Tax Themselves for the Purchase of Text Books.

Jefferson City, Mo., Jan. 20.—Gov. Dockery, in a message to the general assembly this morning, declared his position regarding free text-books.

He recommends the submission of a constitutional amendment authorizing counties, townships or school districts to tax themselves for the purchase of text-books for the free use of pupils. In effect, the governor proposes local option, The message follows:

To the Senate and House of Representatives:

The cost of text-books for the children of our public schools, during the last six years amounted to nearly $3,000,000, or an average annual outlay of about 70 cents for each pupil enrolled.

The present system by which text-books have been furnished under contract has been maintained during the last twelve years. Its purpose is to secure uniformity and to reduce prices for school books.

About one-half of the states of the union have adopted the "state uniformity" system, thus enabling the schools to be better graded and articulated and the people to secure fairly reasonable rates in the purchase of school materials. The books now in use in the public schools of Missouri were contracted under a law approved March 31, 1897, authorizing their adoption for "five years, and until otherwise provided by law." In the absence of additional legislation no other text-books can be legally sold to the children or used in the public schools.

It appears from the able report of Superintendent Carrington that the books selected by the commission in 1897 have in the main been satisfactory, but it is thought that the list should now be revised. There have been difficulties in some parts of the state in securing books when needed, and it is thought that action should be taken looking to a reduction of the present prices.

Obviously, it is the duty of the general assembly to enact such legislation as will secure the very best school books, at the lowest prices, to be furnished to the schools without delay and unnecessary annoyance to the patrons.

In my opinion, the contemplated revision of text-books and attendant reduction of prices should be committed, under wise and exacting safeguards, to a commission, clothed with full authority to deal with this whole question, with the single purpose of promoting our splendid educational system. Missouri's public schools are not excelled by those of any other state of this republic, and our children are entitled to the very best text-books, at the lowest possible cost. Great care should be taken in the legislation enacted to accomplish these desired results. There should be no element of chance. The enactments on this question should clearly be in the interest of our people, whose aim has ever been to afford the youth of this state only that which is best in educational advantages and facilities.

In submitting this recommendation for a text-book commission, I shall not present further argument, inasmuch as this important question has been so fully and so impartially discussed in the annual report of the state superintendent of schools.

In this connection I desire to advert briefly to the suggestion that books should be furnished to the children of the state without cost.

Properly speaking, there can be no such thing as "free text-books." Some one must print them, and some one must pay for them.

Until very recently no other plan was proposed than that the parents should purchase the books. It is now proposed by some people that this duty shall devolve upon the state. After the proposed system is fully installed, at a cost exceeding one million of dollars, it will require from $500,000 to $700,000 annually to maintain them.

Massachusetts was the first state to provide for "district ownership" of text-books for the free use of public school children. This new departure was made in 1884. Under this system the books are paid for by taxing the people of the district. Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania, Nebraska and six other states require every district to purchase and own text-books. Many other states have what is known as "local option ownership," leaving it to each county, township or district, as the case may be, to determine whether it will tax itself for this purpose.

It is proposed that Missouri shall supply school books, free of charge, to all the children, the purchase to be made by the state out of the state revenue fund. This proposition is impracticable under our present constitution, which now limits the levy for state revenue purposes to 15 cents on the $100 valuation, one-third of which is returned to the people to maintain the schools.

It is estimated that the receipts into the state revenue fund will not exceed $5,500,000 during present biennial period. Every dollar of this income will be absolutely required to meet existing demands upon our state revenue fund. It is not wise to enfeeble and enervate our eleemosynary, educational and penal institutions by diverting any part of this income to new objects requiring large appropriations, it matters not how worthy they may be.

I desire to emphasize the treasury situation by reiterating the statement that the estimated income of $5,500,000 for the biennial period upon which we are entering is scarcely sufficient to meet existing liabilities and properly equip and main-
bliminal period upon which we are entering is scarcely sufficient to meet existing liabilities and properly equip and maintain the institutions Missouri has already authorized.

The state should not dissipate its resources and imperil the growth and efficiency of its institutions by entering upon new fields of endeavor, requiring extensive appropriations, unless at the same time the necessary revenue is provided to meet the new liabilities. Concentration of effort and intelligent care and oversight of existing institutions are preferable to the dissipation of our income.

I am a zealous friend of the public school system, but nothing can justify the state in failing to provide ample and increasing facilities for the care of the insane, the feeble-minded, the deaf, the blind and other unfortunate classes of our people.

In view, therefore, of the constitutional limitation upon the taxing power, I recommend the submission of a constitutional amendment authorizing counties, townships or school districts to tax themselves for the purchase of text-books for the free use of pupils. Respectfully,

A. M. DOCKERY, Governor.

State of Missouri, Executive Department

Grafton Chamber Maid Accuses Him of Attempt at Criminal Assault.
Grafton, W. Va., March 21.—Benjamin Riley, the colored day cook at the Painter boarding house and restaurant on Main street, was arrested Thursday night in the opera house on a warrant sworn out by Rubana Decker, a chambermaid employed at the Painter house, charging him with criminal assault. Riley was given a preliminary hearing before Squire Wells but waived examination and was remanded to jail to await the action of the grand jury. GRAFTON.
GRAFTON, W. Va., March 21.—At nine o'clock last night the Painter boarding house was the scene of a revolting crime, which, when made known, startled the citizens into such a rage that a lynching was scarcely avoided. Ben Riley, the negro day cook, caught Miss Ruhana Becker, domestic, making up a bed upstairs, and threw her on the bed and attempted rape. She immediately attempted to scream for help but the brute choked her into insensibility, and while in that state performed his fiendish purpose. In a few minutes the lady recovered and was notified by the negro, with a razor in his right hand, if she made known what had happened he would cut her throat. After Riley left the room, Miss Decker made known the facts and Mr. Painter at once secured a warrant for his arrest. He was located in the opera house and placed in jail over night, and to-day arraigned before Squire Wells, who, after hearing the testimony by Miss Decker and the day clerk, held him to await the action of the grand jury. The young lady came to this city a year ago and has borne a good reputation, and when her comrades learned the facts a lynching was scarcely averted.

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

SUFFOLK, VA., Dec. 10.—Tried by the light of the fire, for whose origin he was alleged to have been responsible, Charles Bynum, a negro, aged about thirty years, was held for court and spirited off to jail to save him from the vengeance of the clamoring crowd which threatened his life.

Justice Morris, near Driver, Va., ten miles from Suffolk, held a hurry session of his court about 3 o'clock this morning in order to give Bynum a preliminary hearing.

Bynum was accused of flirting the barn and stables of John L. Bond, about 10 o'clock last night. The evidence against him is circumstantial, but strong.

Bynum lived in one of Bond's houses, but refused to work or pay rent. He would slip in at night and steal away early in the morning. Yesterday Bond had Bynum locked out. Bynum could not account for his whereabouts, and, besides, he is said to have made threats.

Justice Morris and Hurricane Branch say Bynum's life was in danger. But for the doubt that he might possibly be innocent of the crime the officers could not have saved him. Even as it was, it required calm counsel and quick action. Branch took the man after trial and hurried to jail by a circuitous route.

Bond lost the entire contents of his barn and stables, except some of his horses.

Impudent Clinton Negro Attempts to Force Social Equality
Clinton, Miss., Jan., 27.—The following incident is a good example of the effect of the president's negro policy on this section: A negro man, Isham Peterson, was cutting wood for A. M. Gill, one of our most respected citizens. "Two Mississippi negroes, one at Forret, and the other Clinton, have come near stretching hemp during the past week and but for the timely intervention of some of the older heads, would have done so. SMALL RACE WAR.
OCCURS AT PERRY HILL CHURCH NEAR BIGBYVILLE.
Tom McDonald and Others from Columbia Have a Shooting Scape With a Crowd of Negroes At a Colored Church.
A difficulty occurred at the Perry Hill colored church, near Bigoyville, Sunday between three or four white men from Columbia, and a number of negroes who were at the church attending meeting, which came near resulting in serious trouble. The white men were Tom McDonald and his father, and D. F. Watson and a white boy name Anner Wither spoon, all from this place.

The colored Baptists of the county were holding a four days' Association convention at the Perry Hill church, and McDonald was conducting a soda pop stand near the church, dispensing cold drinks to the crowd of negroes. McDonald, who operates the hack from Columbia to Mt. Pleasant, had his goods in his hack, which he had converted into a sort of stand.

During the day the proprietor became involved in a dispute with a Columbia negro named Dave Jackson, who it is said, refused to pay for a drink. The dispute terminated in McDonald striking the negro a very violent blow in the head, knocking him down. It is said that brass knucks were much in evidence, but whether McDonald used them cannot be said. The fight attracted the attention of the negroes at the church, who went down to McDonald's stand and notified him that he would have to move. He began to arrange to do so, when he or some of the men with him was struck by stones thrown by the angry negroes. McDonald warned them to stop, but they refused to do so. He then pulled his pistol, it is stated, and notified them that he would fire into them if any more stones were thrown. This warning was not effective and McDonald began to fire. He fired three or four shots and a negro named Lewis Thompson was struck on the hand. The party then left and as the hack started down the road it was pursued by several negroes who continued to pelt it with rocks. McDonald again brought his gun into play, firing two more shots, which emptied his revolver. This time the shots were returned by a negro in the crowd who had a pistol. None of the shots took effect. Having exhausted his pistol, and the negroes still pursuing them. McDonald and party left the hack in charge of Gibson, who was driving, and fled into a corn field, through which they were pursued for half a mile or more. The negroes then captured the hack and held it some time. Finally, however, they left and McDonald and party recovered it and returned to town. It was stated that the negroes intended having McDonald and his party arrested Monday, but at 12 o'clock nothing had been done.

From last reports the young woman was in a critical condition.

The negro, after committing the deed, left the scene. He is well known by those around Darien Junction. He was captured by Agent Rooney at Everett City early this morning, but before he could be identified, escaped.

OCCURED AT DARIEN JUNCT.
Negro Was Captured at Everett City Yesterday Morning, But Escaped.—Posses are Now Scouring Woods.
Minnie Johnson, a young white girl residing near Darien Junction, on the Darien & Western railroad, was beaten into insensibility and then assaulted by a negro Thursday morning, news of which reached this city yesterday.

The rash deed has caused considerable excitement in the vicinity in which it occurred, and a lynching may yet occur as a result.

The story was told to a News reporter yesterday by J. D. Rooney, agent of the Southern and Seaboard at Everett City.

It seems that the act was committed near the home of the girl at the above stated place.

As soon as the negro accomplished his purpose, he made for the woods. The different agents along the line of the Seaboard were notified of the affair. Agent Rooney, who has assisted in the arrest of many criminals. at Everett, kept a sharp watch for the negro, and it is his impression that he once had the rascal, but he escaped.

Yesterday morning early a strange negro was seen lounging around Everett. Mr. Rooney at once took charge of the negro, but he succeeded in escaping later in the day. He was followed by several around Everett, and several shots were fired at the fleeing negro, but none took effect, and he succeeded in getting in the swamps.

After Agent Rooney had received a description of the negro charged with the crime, he was quite sure that the man he had captured at Everett was the one wanted, as he answered the description in every particular.

Severad posses were soon organized at Darien Junction and other places on the road and last night the woods were being scoured for the negro. It was learned that he was surrounded near Mt. Pleasant. The mob, so it was stated, were determined to lynch the negro if they succeeded in capturing him, and he may have already paid for the rash act.

Several telephonic communications were received in the city yesterday, asking for the county hounds, but as they are over near Fancy Bluff it was impossible to get them to Everett. It is undersood, however, that hounds will be secured at Jesup this morning and will be placed on the trail of the negro if he was not captured last night.

The negro gave his name as Louis Olsen. He weighs about 160 pounds, 5 feet 10 inches tall; is of dark ginger cake color; small mustache, very thick lips; wore a double-breasted blue shirt, resembling a jumper, brown striped pants, shoes badly worn, a brown cap.

It is understood that his victim was in a critical condition yesterday and was not expected to recover.

The negro, whose correct name is thought to be Ed Claus, has been employed by the railorad and was recently working near Crescent.

The affair has caused considerable excitement near Darien Junction, and if the negro is captured he will hardly be tried by the courts.
ed-claus-darien-junction-1903-07-10.A6:
VICTIM IS IN DARIEN.
It Was Thought That Miss Johnson Will Recover.
Will Recover.

Därlen, Ga., July 11.—Miss Minnie Johnson the victim of the negro fiend, Ed. Claus, is now in Darien under treatment of physicians. Her condition is serious, but it is now thought she will recover.

The crime was committed about twelve miles from this city, and was one of the most revolting of the long list of such crimes committed in the South. Miss Johnson was living with the family of Mr. Forbes at Oak Hill, a station on the Darien and Western Railroad. Early Thursday morning, before the family was up, Miss Johnson rose and in attending to her duties went near the woods, about 200 yards from the house. While there she was suddenly confronted by the negro, who choked her and beat her into insensibility. She was dragged into the woods, where the negro accomplished his purpose and left her for dead. Later she was missed, and a search, resulted in her discovery in the woods.

The negro was a stranger in the community having recently come from Glenn county. He is said to have burglarized a store there two days before his appearance in this county. A reward of $200 has been offered by the county commissioners, and a similar amount may be offered by the state unless the negro has been captured.

This is the first crime of this kind committed in this community, and both whites and blacks are shocked at its enormity.

In the course of a fight between David W. Ellington surrendered only after his house had been surrounded by police, some of them armed with shotguns, and the doors and windows had been splintered by bullets.

His niece, Mattie Gilland, 12 years old, was sent as a courier to tell the police that her uncle, Ellington, wished to surrender.

When Ellington appeared at the door to let the policemen arrest him, he held in his hand a revolver still containing three cartridges. He was covered by a double-barreled shotgun in the hands of Sergeant Con Bolland and made no attempt to fire.

Patrolman Peter Dolan, who was wounded early in the engagement, was removed to his home, No. 6401 Manchester avenue. Doctor R. C. Blackmer of No. 6776 Manchester avenue says he is not dangerously hurt. One bullet entered the arm between the elbow and wrist, a second struck him in the upper arm and a third grazed his left side, inflicting only a slight abrasion.

DIED IN AMBULANCE.

Chambliss died in an ambulance on the way to the City Hospital. He was shot through the back.

The fight was precipitated by Ellington's attempt to kill Edward Ferguson of No. 6930 Glades avenue, and David Vertres of No. 6655 Manchester avenue, at each of whom he fired a shot from a revolver.

POLICEMAN USES ONE ARM.

Dolan, though wounded, was using his right arm alternately in holding the prisoner and discharging his revolver. Another volley from Ellington sent both Dolan and Chambliss to the ground, and left McGrath to take care of both.

On the arrival of Patrolmen James Macklin, John Stone and Eugene O'Connor, in charge of Sergeant Con Bolland, the latter ordered his men to visit the houses of white residents near the scene and secure shotguns. Quick Trials for Lynchings.
Judge Richardson of the Second circuit has an opportunity to apply the restricting bill in Lowndes, where a regular term of the Circuit court will not be held until February. Under the provisions of that bill Judge Richardson can by a mere entry in the minutes of the court at Hayneville instantly convene a special term and summon a grand jury.

The trouble in Lowndes arose over the possession of some bales of cotton, and it shows how readily and easily anarchy can be carried from one crime to another. The negroes who had the cotton were anarchistic at the outset, and now their pursuers are filled with the demoralizing spirit.

The state has had but one lynching this year, and if another occurs in Lowndes it will not be because of the law's delay. The machinery of the law can now be rendered as speedy and efficient as the most bloodthirsty can desire. A special term can try the negroes in an hour's time, and such a trial should satisfy even those who desire a hanging as a means of excitement.

Let us hope that between the new law and the cool sense of the people of Lowndes the state will not be disgraced by a second lynching. If a trial could not be had until February, there would be some excuse for pleading the law's delay, but under the law as it stands any such excuse is out of the question. The law is not only speedy—it is instantaneous, always provided the Circuit judge will act up to the spirit of the new law. Judge Richardson lives at Greenville, about twenty miles from Hayneville, the county seat of Lowndes.

A NEGRO LYNCHED
HE WAS PULLED TO THE LIMB OF A TREE.
He Assaulted Tom McDade of Bossier. Fired at and Shot Harvey Connell, the Overseer.
Tuesday morning shortly after 6 o'clock a tragedy was enacted on the old Knox Point plantation in Bossier about twenty miles below Shreveport. A long drawn out statement may be summarized in these words: Jim Brown, a negro, occupied a cabin on the plantation where he was employed. When awakened by Mr. Connell, the overseer, he replied that he would not go to work as his brother was in trouble. On reporting this fact to Mr. McDade, who is the owner of the plantation, Mr. Connell, was directed to return to the negro's cabin and come with him to the lot where he would give him his time. Jim Brown dragged along in a sulky mood, muttering to himself, until he reached Mr. McDade who upbraided him for his laziness. The negro rejoined with impudent words. Connell had started to the commissary to get Brown's time when he was startled by McDade calling him, "Harvey! Harvey!" and as he faced about saw the negro and Mr. McDade struggling desperately. The negro held a six-shooter in his right hand. As Connell rushed towards the combatants he could not fire without endangering McDade. Suddenly the negro released his grasp on McDade and fired at Connell, who was shot in the forearm, and a second shot struck him in the leg. Connell was disabled and powerless to defend himself or to assist McDade. The negro then jumped aside and fired at McDade and ran away. As the negro was fleeing he was shot in the leg by Connell, who had emptied his pistol.

A posse of white men was organized and after a brisk ride Jim Brown was captured, disarmed and hanged to a tree near McDade station on the Shreveport and Red River Valley road about half a mile distant from the place where the negro had shot Connell.

The negro was regarded with disfavor. He was shiftless and a disturber of the peace, and in the moment of excitement the outraged citizens became the judge, the jury and the executioner at one and the same time. Such action is not surprising and is the result arising from the apprehension of danger when a desperate and lawless man is a menace to the peace and well being of a community.

Mr. Connell is at the Sanitarium where he is receiving the best attention. Fortunately he was not seriously wounded and he will recover speedily.

As yet the negro, or negroes who did the shooting have not been arrested. There were four in the party, but only two of them participated in the shooting, each of them firing one shot. Night Foreman.

Waite, who was night foreman of the Birmingham Pipe and Casting company, was returning home with Allen Cleburne, a negro, who was employed in the works. As they reached Thirty-second street and First avenue they passed four negroes. Just after they had passed the negroes, Cleburne turned and saw that one of the four had a pistol pointed at them. He cried to Waite to run for his life, but the white man had scarcely moved when he was shot through the chest and the left arm.

It seems that one of the negroes in the party had a grudge against Waite for discharging him from the works, and as the party passed Waite in the road he turned and, cursing, said:

A KENTUCKY SOLUTION.
THE HERALD desires to call attention of the race problem theorists to the way they handle such things in the ordinarily peaceful little city of Henderson, in the good old state of Kentucky. We feel sure they will be interested in the following item from the Henderson Journal:

"Henderson had a small touch of race war fever at Central park Sunday night. A large number of citizens, white and black, were enjoying that popular resort, and the seats were nearly all occupied. A negro woman made remarks in the presence of or toward a white lady, which were of somewhat insulting nature, which were resented by the lady's escort. The negress had no sooner got the words "I'm as good as any white lady" out of her mouth than the gentleman escort struck her. Other whites in the park took up the fever and proceeded to drive other negroes from the park, which they did in short order, and peace soon settled upon the scene."

Thus decently and in order was the thing done. The colored lady made the definite announcement that she was as good as any white lady south of the Ohio river. Here was a casus belli. One more sharply defined could not be laid down. Why, the idea of a colored lady being as good as a white lady in any sense of the word is enough to exasperate every white gentleman in the south. And, of course, the white lady's escort promptly proved that the colored lady was not as good as his particular white lady by whacking the colored lady across the mouth.

At this juncture, according to the report, the trouble began. There is no evidence that there were any real hostilities, aside from the smacking administered to the colored lady. We are inclined to believe that the colored brothers and sisters were gently pushed out of the park and dispersed to their several homes. Anyway, we are told that "peace soon settled upon the scene," from which it is fair to infer that not a negro was in sight.

How much better this method of procedure is than the one in vogue in Indiana, in Illinois and in other northern states. There the negroes are hanged and shot, sometimes burned at stakes. In Kentucky they are merely pushed out and away.

Postmistress at Indianola, Miss., Driven to Resign by a Lawless Element.
Washington, Jan. 3.—The feature of the cabinet meeting yesterday was the decision to close permanently the postoffice at Indianola, Miss., from which the postmistress, Minnie M. Cox, colored, resigned under compulsion a few days ago.

The postmaster general is satisfied that the woman was obliged to resign under duress; in fact, that her life was endangered. The cabinet, after a long discussion, decided that the office will not be reopened until the people in the district are ready to accept this woman as their postmistress.

Secretary Cortelyou, for the president, made public the following:

"The postmaster at Indianola, Miss., is Mrs. Minnie W. Cox, a colored woman. She served three years as postmaster under President Harrison. When President McKinley came in she was again appointed in 1897, nearly six years ago. Her character and standing in the community are indorsed by the best and most reputable people in the town. Among those on her bond is the present democratic state senator from the district, together with the leading banker of Indianola and an ex-state senator from the district, also a democrat. The postmaster and her husband own from $10,000 to $15,000 worth of property in Sunflower county.

"The reports of postoffice inspectors who have investigated the office from time to time show that she has given the utmost satisfaction to all the patrons of the office; that she is at all times courteous, faithful, competent and honest in the discharge of her duties. Her moral standing in the community is of the highest. Her reputation is of the best. Few offices of this grade in any state are conducted better.

"The postmaster recently forwarded her resignation, to take effect on Jan. 1, but the report of inspectors and information received from various reputable white citizens of the town and neighborhood show that the resignation was forced by a brutal and lawless element, purely upon the ground of her color, and was obtained under terror of threats. The mayor of the town and the sheriff of the county both told the postoffice inspector that if she refused to resign they could not be answerable for her safety, although at the same time not one word was said against her. On Jan. 1 the bondsmen of the postmaster telegraphed that the postoffice was closed; that the postmaster claimed that her resignation was in the president's hands, to take effect Jan. 1, and that there had been no advice of the appointment of her successor. "Prompt action necessary by the president for the relief of the business interests, which are being injured solely by the action of the lawless element of the town, is wholly secondary to the preservation of law and order and the assertion of the fundamental principle that this government will not connive at or tolerate wrong and outrage of such flagrant character."

"The postmaster's resignation has been received but not accepted. In view of the facts the postoffice at Indianola is closed. All mail for that place will be forwarded to Greenville. The case will be referred to the attorney general."

The sowing of the wind made the reaping thus, as it does always, of the whirlwind.

Negro Leaves the Neighborhood at the Mob's Behest and the White Women Are Under Orders to Depart.
CLOSING OF A TRUST MILL
TERRE HAUTE WILL LOSE A VERY IMPORTANT INDUSTRY.
Lutheran Church Dedicated at Hammond-Evansville Needs a Juvenile Court-Other Indiana News.
BLOOMINGTON, Ind., April 26.—Twelve masked men, carrying bundles of switches, visited the house of Rebecca and Annie Stevens, two middle-aged white women who live a mile north of this city, this morning at 1 o'clock and dragged from the house a negro—Joe Shively—who had been living there several weeks. Shively was roughly handled, taken to a grove of trees near the house, tied to a sapling and severely beaten.

A few minutes afterward the two white women and Shively's sister, a young colored girl, were taken from the house, stripped to the waist, and whipped until the blood ran. The mob was led by a tall man, whose orders were obeyed implicitly. He allowed no talking and the punishment given the four was administered in silence, only the screams of the victims being heard by terrified neighbors.

The Stevens house has borne a bad reputation in this community. It was learned by the members of the mob that a negro had been living at the house for some time on terms of perfect equality with the white women. His sister also was there. Stories of more or less unprintable nature were afloat, and rumors that the people in the house would be severely dealt with had been whispered around. So far as known no warning of the proposed visit of the white-cappers had been given to the Stevens women.

The belief here is that the twelve men that composed the mob are citizens of Bloomington of excellent character. Some names are whispered about with the utmost caution. It is said that public opinion became so aroused at the condition of affairs that a trip to the house was decided on and the details quietly planned.

After being lashed fully fifty times Shively was ordered to leave the county, and it is said that he obeyed the mandate at once. The Stevens women were ordered to depart, it is said, but it is not known whether they have gone.

The whitecapping has created great excitement here, and sentiment seems to be with the unknown visitors to the Stevens home.

"Unless I am given definite assurance by the people of Monroe county and Bloomington that they intend to suppress anarchy with an iron hand and that the perpetrators of the outrage upon helpless women Sunday morning will be exposed and punished I shall propose to the next Legislature the removal of the State University from a community that permits it to be disgraced."

This clean-cut statement from Governor Durbin is precisely indicative of his indignation over the whitecapping that took place at Bloomington early Sunday morning when twelve masked men, said to be reputable citizens of the university town, visited the home of Rebecca and Annie Stevens, white women, and whipped them, together with Joe Shiveley, colored, and Shiveley's sister. The outrage took place almost within the shadow of the State University buildings.

GOVERNOR'S WRATH.

Governor Durbin has taken the position that it is time for whitecapping to cease in Indiana, and although handicapped and blocked in several cases by the apathy or positive sympathy of citizens with whitecappers he has worked untiringly under discouraging conditions to bring whitecappers under the finger of the law. This last outrage has set his wrath flaming, and he declares without any evasion that Bloomington must not suffer whitecappers to escape punishment this time and must not permit such brutalities in the future or he will bend every influence of the executive office toward having the State University removed to a city where its name will not be tarnished.

"This outrage," continued the Governor yesterday, "is the most disgraceful exhibition that has occurred to disgust and anger decent citizens. It does not matter what offense these women committed; that does not enter into it at all. The plain fact remains that they were seized in their helplessness by big, brutal men who exposed them to indignities and then lashed them barbarously in the fashion of the middle ages. This sort of thing has got to stop if I have to use state troops to do it.

"Passing the barbarity of the crime itself, it was done almost within the confines of the campus of Indiana University, where boys and girls are sent by their parents to learn how to be good men and women and lawabiding citizens. SHERIFF THRASHER PROTESTS AGAINST EXECUTIVE'S CRITICISMS.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

BLOOMINGTON, Ind., April 28.—There is intense interest here throughout the city over the recent reported "whitecapping" here and the public announcement of Governor Durbin in which he says unless the public officials make effort to enforce the laws that he will recommend to the next Legislature that the university be removed from here. A careful investigation here by leading citizens has proved beyond doubt that the Stevens girl and the colored man, Shiveley, were whipped by a drunken crowd of rowdies who had been frequenting this house and others of questionable nature in the same proximity.

As soon as the reports became generally known that the people had been whipped, the court officers instituted a court of inquiry which is making a rigid examination of all who can in any way have knowledge of the affair. This has already proved that the men in the crowd had been in the habit of frequenting the place, that they were not masked and were intoxicated, and that the trouble Saturday night was because the woman had refused them admission to the place. The people were then taken and cruelly whipped. That the crowd was composed of any respectable citizens or an organized mob, is not true, and is even denied by the victims, who say that all of them they recognized had been frequenters of their society. Judge Wilson and other court officers are sparing no effort to bring the guilty men to justice, and it is likely that arrests will follow in a few days.

Sheriff Trasher has mailed a letter to Governor Durbin, in answer to a telegram finding fault with his enforcement of law and demanding that he do his duty as an officer. In closing the letter the sheriff says: "There has not been a warrant in my hands for a whitecap but has been served and served promptly. If ever any man belonging to any whitecap band or mob was favored in the Monroe Circuit Court, I don't and can't call it to mind.

"I am informed since receiving your message, that the trouble last Saturday night was only a row in a house of bad repute. I can't say as to the truth of this report. All that I can say to you is that I am ready to make any and all arrests when I am furnished a warrant, and no man can say that I ever failed to do my whole duty when called upon. If these people who are corresponding with you will furnish the officers here with information sufficient to procure a warrant, I feel safe in saying to Your Honor that I have the confidence in our judge, the Hon. J. B. Wilson, and in the prosecutor, the Hon. R. G. Miller, that they will do their whole duty as promptly as any officers in the State of Indiana. If Your Honor remembers the noted John Cole case it was promptly and vigorously dealt with by the prosecutor, R. G. Miller, and I will say to you—and the records of Monroe county will bear me out in this statement—that there has never been a whitecap favored by the officers of the Monroe Circuit Court."

The following editorial in the Daily Telephone of this city, the leading Republican paper of the county, clearly expresses the sentiment of the community:

"Upon this alleged 'whitecapping' being reported and again when Governor Durbin sent his demand to Sheriff Thrasher the editor of the Telephone made a personal investigation with other citizens, closely questioning the colored man who seems to be the cause of the trouble. Now for the facts. A colored man lives in adjoining rooms in a house with a white woman and three daughters. In the same proximity are alleged disreputable places. Not infrequently on Saturday nights rough characters intoxicated are about these houses, and last Saturday night between 1 and 2 o'clock a number of such drunken men not masked called at this particular house, knocked the door open and the colored man and girls were taken out and cruelly beaten. The police were called, but by that time the men had escaped. The colored man was at work as usual Monday and also the girls. The men were not masked, are known to the people, had been callers at the house before, made no attempt to conceal their object, were intoxicated and were men without character or reputation. The facts show that the occurrence of Saturday night was a drunken row of men at a questionable place that they had before visited in a like manner and for a like purpose. It is not to be excused, but is an offense that must be punished. It was not what people know as 'whitecapping.' It was not an organized band of masked men—of leading citizens—but of drunken rowdies, just such an occurrence as may happen in any town or city in the State and with which good citizens can in no possible way be connected.

"Such reports are a great injustice to our community, our people and the university, but the Governor is not to be criticised in his firm rebuke if the facts substantiated the reports. A strike of fifty molders in the Home Stove Company's factory will begin this morning. The strike has been sanctioned by the International Iron Molders' Union of North America, and will not end until the demands made by the molders are acceded to by the proprietors of the foundry. The strike may possibly throw the 175 men employed in the foundry out of employment, as without the molders at work in the foundry, the other department of the stove works will be unable to accomplish much.

The trouble from which the strike has arisen has been brewing for the last three weeks. At that time a demand for an increase of 10 per cent. was made on the local stove manufactories and agreed to by the Indianapolis Stove Company, conditioned on a similar increase being granted by its competitors in this field. The Home Stove Company, through its president, George G. Alig, declared that it would not grant the increase, and the sanction for the strike was obtained from the headquarters of the union in Cincinnati by telephone yesterday afternoon. During its progress the strike will be conducted by George Webber, Frank Reuf, Henry McDaniels, Ben Bachman and Bart Flynn, a strike committee, and supervised by George Custer, business agent of the molders' union. The molders during the strike will receive the benefits of the union, a weekly wage allowed them, and the men will not return to work until a settlement is made based on the proposition which was re-refused.

The molders made a proposal to the stove men that they would agree to the report made by a committee of three, one member from the molders, one from the manufacturers and one to be disinterested, on the prices for labor paid in other communities, and abide by the recommendations made. The Home Stove Company refused to consent to this plan, and firmly declared that the increase would not be granted.

The molders wish to bring the price of labor paid in Indianapolis up to that paid in other competitive fields. Indianapolis molders now receive $1.10, board rate, for work, while for similar work at other places the price paid is $1.20. The prices in other fields agree with the standards established by the conference of the Stove Founders' National Defensive Association and the molders' union, while in Indianapolis the lower price has been operative.

Luling, La., Jan. 26.—John Thomas, a negro, who murdered Sheriff Louis S. Oury, of St. Charles Parish, was shot to death and his body burned by a mob of several hundred men this afternoon.

AGAIN NIGHT HAS FALLEN
And in Darkness Such as Hid His Face From His Helpless Victim, Osborne is Halted on His Journey to Take One Darker From Which There is No Return.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Charlotte, N. C., July 3.—John Osborne, the negro charged with criminally assaulting Mrs. Lizzie Wentz, in Union county, Saturday night, paid the penalty with his life. Last night he was taken from the officers who were conveying him to the Union county jail and lynched at a point about two miles from Indian Trail, a station on the Carolina Central railroad.

The lynching party was composed of several hundred people, and the two men who had charge of the prisoner were easily over-powered. Osborne received a preliminary hearing during the afternoon and was committed to jail to await the next term of Union county Superior court. It is said that the negro confessed to the crime before he was lynched.

After the evidence had been concluded Esquire Broom committed him to jail without bond. Messrs. Frank Kezziah and Luke Horton were deputized to take the prisoner to Monroe and lodge him in jail.

Darkness had now set in and Messrs. Kezziah and Horton thought it better to drive to Indian Trail, a distance of about three miles, and board the eastbound Seaboard Air Line train. Accordingly they placed the negro after securely binding him with ropes in a buggy and started to the station.

After they had traveled about two miles of the distance, and when they were in the midst of a body of dense woodland, they were halted by several men, who suddenly stepped out into the road from behind trees.

Mr. Kezziah, who was driving, demurred, but before he had spoken half a dozen words he was seized and dragged from the buggy by two stalwart men.

At this juncture the road was filled with men, and when Mr. Kezziah fired a pistol at the man who had taken him from the buggy, a number of shots hummed from the crowd, which appeared to number several hundred men.

When Mr. Horton came to the assistance of Mr. Kezziah, the negro had been pulled from the buggy and seized by several men.

The community, of course, is greatly stirred up by the brutal crime and the lynching which followed, and while there is regret that the county of Union has been stained by a lynching, not a voice has been raised in protest against the swift vengeance which was visited upon the negro brute.

Even the people of Osborne's own race are a unit in affirming that the victim of the mob's fury got no more than his just deserts.

Some of the persons most active in hunting up evidence against the perpetrator of the crime were negroes, several of whom told Osborne that he ought to pay the penalty of death for his crime.

One of the principal witnesses for the prosecution was a negro woman who lives on Mrs. Wentz's farm, and after telling Osborne that he deserved to be lynched, she charged him with attempting the same crime on a negro woman a short time ago.

The evidence against Osborne was entirely circumstantial, but it was so complete in its entirety as to leave no room for doubt as to his guilt.

Though Osborne worked for Mr. Joe Biggers, who lived ten miles away from where Mrs. Wentz lived, near Indian Trail, he was the first man and the only man upon whom suspicion fell; and within 48 hours after the crime was committed this suspicion came to be a belief in the minds of all people—white and colored—who lived in the neighborhood of where the crime was committed. He had a bad character generally speaking and a few years ago had been charged with attempting to assault another white woman, a Mrs. Hargett, but, apart from his previous bad record, the evidence connecting him with the assault on Mrs. Wentz became insistently cumulative and vividly strong.

STRONG CIRCUMSTANTIAL EVIDENCE.

It was proven that on the night the crime was committed Osborne had hidden a mule within a quarter of a mile of Mrs. Wentz's home, and he was tracked from where he had bitched the mule to the home of his victim. In his Sunday vest pocket was found a small piece of string that Mrs. Wentz recognized as the same bit of twine that she had kept in a match box in her house. She remembered that in looking for money the negro had struck a number of matches. And in the pockets of Osborne was found, too, money that it was alleged he must have taken from Mrs. Wentz.

In the preliminary trial that was given Osborne at the home of Mrs. Wentz Thursday evening more than 20 witnesses testified, and the testimony, linked together, left the colored witnesses standing up in the shady grove and declaring that the prisoner was guilty.

THE OPINION OF A MOTHER.

Even Osborne's own mother, who came to the scene, yelled aloud:

"John, you know you are guilty. Good-bye. There ain't nothin' for you to do but pray."

When the prosecution, which was represented by Mr. Plummer Stewart, of this city, a nephew of Mrs. Wentz, had finished, there was a muttered sentiment in the outskirts of the crowd that boded ill for the prisoner. The manner of the deed had been such as to arouse to anger the most conservative people in the audience. Mrs. Wentz is 64 years old; a feeble, timid woman, who lives alone—saving the presence of an aged negro woman, who lives in a hut in the yard. It was the voice of this negress that Osborne had imitated, crying that he was ill—to let him in the house. When the door had been opened he had clutched Mrs. Wentz by the throat, and had become a flend in violence and horrid language. Such little money as he could find—less than a dollar in all—he had taken with him.

A NERVOUS COLLAPSE.

Before his accusers the criminal almost collapsed in his excessive fright. He was young—only 24 years old and black as the pure Ethiopian type, but his politeness, his eager desire to propitiate everyone who came near him would have been pitiable if it had not been ghastly. Just before he was arrested he had come trembling like a reed in the wind to Mr. Plummer Stewart and had begged to be allowed to shake hands. Fawning like a whipped cur he maintained until death this attitude of extreme humility and courtesy.

Brought From Edgecombe for Safe Keeping in Raleigh Jail.
Charged with rape, Joseph Battle, a negro man about twenty-eight years old, was brought to Raleigh yesterday morning and put in Wake county jail for safe keeping.

He was brought here by Deputy Sheriff B. R. Height, of Edgecombe county who reports that the feeling in Edgecombe was so high against the negro that it was thought best to bring him to Raleigh and avoid trouble.

Battle is the negro charged with committing an outrage on Mrs. Bettie Long, a white woman of Edgecombe county on the first of last August. He escaped to Virginia, was caught at Manchester and was taken back to Tarboro from which place he was brought to Raleigh.

Immediately after the commission of the horrible crime a posse was formed to capture the negro, but he escaped and when located in Virginia was brought back on requisition papers, a deputy going from Edgecombe after him. When he was back in the county feeling again ran high and it was decided best to get him quietly out of Edgecombe as the officers heard intimations that an attempt would be made to get the negro and lynch him.

The deputy and the negro had an exciting drive and Mr. Height states that in order to escape a possible attempt to catch the man, as he understood that sentinels had been posted at various points to head him off, he took a round-about course and drove over 66 miles out of a direct road in order to save the man's life.

Battle is a bad looking negro, though he is dressed fairly well. He will be kept here till the next term of Edgecombe court which will come next March.

PRISONERGAVEALARM
Among the Desperadoes is Joe Battle, Charged With Rape, a Federal Prisoner and Lynn Spence Indicted for Burglary by Grand Jury.
As easily as if no steel bars and brick walls surrounded them nine negroes confined in Wake County jail left that place yesterday morning between three and four o'clock.

Among the nine prisoners who escaped are some desperate characters, men who before this have been in jails and the penitentiary, whidle one was here for safe keeping, charged with rape in Edgecombe county, another was a Federal prisoner, and another a negro already indicted for burglary and to be tried for his life.

The nine negroes who escaped are Dan Biggs, John Bethel, Ed. Cotten, Henry Curtis, George Hayes, Mooney Perry, Len Spence, Herbert Raynor and Joe Battle. One has been recaptured, Hubert Ravner, the Federal prisoner, but the others are all still at large, though word came late yesterday afternoon that Perry was in the neighborhood of Rogers' store, in the northern part of the county.

HOW IT WAS DONE.

It was between three and four o'clock when the negroes escaped and investigation shows that they had had fixed so that others might escape. It was one of these, John Smith, a one-armed negro who, getting out of the jail woke the cook, who slept in the jail yard, and with him went to Jailer Parham's house to tell of the wholesale delivery.

By some means one of the men in the steel corridor on the lower floor of the jail, which encloses three cells, had come into possession of a knife which he had worked so as to make a jagged saw, or by some it is thought he had a steel file. With this one of the lock bars to the inside cell had been partly sawed in half, and then by some means snapped off. This gave play to the lock levers of two of the cell doors, which were opened, though the men in the third cell were still confined as the lock lever on it would not work.

Once these levers were broken it was easy to use the piece to break off another section riveted on, and with this the negroes broke out, piece by piece, a section of an inner cell. The steel bar used and the pieces broken out show that great force was used, and that perhaps all nine of the prisoners put their weight on the bar in breaking the steel cross pieces riveted together, forming the side of the cell. It is a cell made by Pually & Brother, of St. Louis, and was easily broken.

A small hole being thus made the men crept outside the steel cell at the back, and were then in a narrow passage way. They worked out a wooden support under a barred window and then with their steel bar broke out the bricks under the window, soon making an opening large enough to slip through. Once in the yard the escape over the fence next to the postoffice back yard.

It is not known that any aid came from the outside, but Jailer Parham says that if the story the negro prisoners tell is true, there was outside aid. They say that John Bethel had a pistol, and that he swore he would shoot anyone who attempted to make an outcry. He had also several knives.

The first that was known of the delivery was when John Smith, one of the prisoners who would not escape, climbed through the hole made by the nine confederates and went to the back yard of the jail and notified the cook. Then the cook and the prisoner went to the residence of Jailer O. L. Parham, just in the rear of the jail, on Salisbury street, and notified him of the occurrence. Jailer Parham immediately called up the Raleigh police and Sheriff Page. Just as they reached the opening in the wall where the men had escaped, John Young, a one-legged negro, had put his head out the hole, but withdrew it when he saw the officers.

A mob was rapidly formed to lynch him, and he fled to Virginia. He was afterwards caught and taken to Tarboro but again a mob formed, but the sheriff and one of his deputies brought the prisoner to Raleigh. He is twenty-two years old.

GRAND LODGE
OF MASONS
Growth of the Order in North Carolina the Largest in Its History.

BALBICH, N. C., Jan. 12—North C.

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

RALEIGH, N. C., Jan. 12.—North Carolina Grand Lodge of Masons convened to-night; over 450 Masons present. Reports of all officers were gratifying and showed 13,663 Masons in the State, there being 340 lodges. The grand secretary's report states that the growth of the order in the State the past year has been the largest in the history of the order in North Carolina.

Colonel J. S. Cuningham, of Person, county, delivered an eloquent oration.

ANNUAL ADDRESS.

The annual address by Grand Master H. I. Clark, of Scotland Neck, declared that the corner-stone of the new temple will certainly be laid in the early spring.

Mrs. Paschal Long came from Tarboro this morning and identified Joe Battle, colored, as the negro who criminally assaulted her last August. Battle has been in jail here the past two months, and was one of the nine prisoners who broke jail recently and were recaptured.

CAPTURED IN MANCHESTER.

Battle is the negro who was captured some months ago in Manchester, Va. Battle will be kept here until his trial, as there is danger of his being lynched if taken to Tarboro.

SEABOARD'S EXCEPTIONS
Denies the Authority of the Corporation Commission to Issue Order.
THE DANGER OF LYNCHING
Sheriffs Take Extra Precaution to Prevent Violence to Joe Battle.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
ALEIGH, N. C. March 5-The 8c

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

RALEIGH, N. C., March 5.—The Seaboard Air Line Railroad has filed exceptions to the order for the Seaboard and Southern to join in a union station in Charlotte. The exceptions are on the ground that the commission has no authority or jurisdiction to issue such an order; that such action is in violation of the fifth amendment to the Constitution of the United States; that the present Seaboard depot at Charlotte is adequate and convenient for the traveling public; that the land owned jointly at the juncture of the two roads, on which the commission orders the union station to be built, is neither adequate or suitable for a union station, and that a union station is in truth neither practicable or needed for the city of Charlotte.

DANGER OF LYNCHING.

The sheriff of Edgecombe county came here yesterday and left last night with Joe Battle, whom he carried back to Tarboro to stand trial for his life on the charge of criminal assault on a respectable white woman near that town. Battle was captured in Virginia soon after the crime, and was brought here for safekeeping. There were threats of lynching if he were carried then to Tarboro. Considerable precaution is to be taken now to prevent any such interference with the law taking its course. Judge Fred Moore is the judge presiding at this term of the Edgecombe Court.

The suit of the Raleigh Hoslery Mill vs. the Seaboard Air Line, now on its third trial in Wake Superior Court, two new trials having been allowed on appeal to the Supreme Court from former trials. The suit is for $26,000 damages by reason of the burning of the mill three years ago. The charge is that a spark from a passing engine set fire to the mill. The insurance has really been paid and the mill rebuilt in another location, so that the suit is really by the insurance companies against the Seaboard Air Line. The railroad won in former suits.

TOBACCO COMPANY.

The Secretary of State charters the Dross Tobacco Company, of Copeland, Surry county, with $100,000 capital authorized and $20,000 subscribed by W. R. Dross and others. The new company will deal in leaf and also do a manufacturing business.

It is given out that a great revival meeting will be inaugurated by the Tabernacle Baptist Church here on the first Sunday in April, and that the preaching will be by one of the most prominent ministers of Virginia. The name of the preacher is withheld, however, for the present.

The North Carolina Naval Stores Company, of Elizabeth City, was granted a charter this morning, the authorized capital being $100,000, and that subscribed $50,000. The concern will make turpentine and other pine products by wood distillation and furnace heat processes. The principal incorporators are J. W. Pritchett and Thomas H. Rollins.

The remains of Mr. George Fleming were brought here for interment this morning from Louisburg, where he died yesterday. He was a brother of Mr. Percy Fleming, teller in the State treasury. He had been in falling health for some time.

A private letter received here from Mrs. Russell is to the effect that the condition of her husband, ex-Governor Daniel L. Russell, is very critical. In fact, there seems to be no hope at all for his recovery, and death is expected at any time. He is in Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, where he underwent an operation for the removal of a diseased kidney.

MYSTERIOUS DEATH ON MOVING TRAIN
Two Negroes Under Arrest and in Danger of Lynching.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
LYNCHBURG, VA., Sept. 11.—William P. Harris, of Iron Gate, was shot and killed early this morning on a freight train of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad, near Gladstone, twenty-five miles east of Lynchburg. Members of the train crew heard several pistol shots as the train was dashing through the night, but they paid no attention to the noise and were not aware that any serious trouble had occurred until the train reached Gladstone, when they found the dead body of Harris lying on a car. He had been shot and evidently instantly killed.

How the dark tragedy occurred is wrapped in mystery. The unfortunate man's watch is missing, but some money which he had was found untouched. Two negroes, Law Young and William Murphey, who are suspected, were arrested here while beating their way west. They were at Gladstone when the body was found. Young and Murphey declare that they know nothing of the shooting.

It is said that there is much excitement at Gladstone, and that a crowd of several hundred people have been waiting there to-day for the arrival of the two negroes. The Lynchburg authorities, however, would not incur the responsibility of carrying the negroes to Gladstone, but they will be taken there tomorrow by a Gladstone official. Trouble is feared. Harris had been with the American Bridge Company in Richmond and was on his way to visit his wife and two children.

SUPPOSED MURDERER

Negro Arrested Charged With Shooting W. P. Harris.

THE EVIDENCE DAMAGING

He Was Brought Back from Gladstone by Detective C. D. Duke, and Was Lodged in the Henrico County Jail.
Frank Bradley, a negro tramp and desperado, arrested at Warminster on Saturday on the charge of murdering W. P Harris, a white bridge-builder, while the two were beating a ride on a west-bound freight near that place in Nelson county early Friday morning, was brought to this city yesterday by Mr. C. D. Duke, a special detective of the Baldwin agency, in company with Mr. W. E. Jones, another officer of the same agency, and lodged in Henrico jail. Mr. Duke went on the case as soon as the dead body of Harris was found lying in his own life blood on top of a box-car, and has secured evidence of a very damaging character against the negro. He is satisfied that he has the right man and the negro's own admissions as to his movements leave little or no doubt of this, though he denies having committed the crime.

REVOLVER ON HIM.

Bradley was first taken in charge by railway employees at Gladstone, Nelson county, on account of the strong suspicion against him, caused by his movements. Before dawn on the morning

On the negro's person were found a revolver and four cartridges, leaving one chamber empty. The weapon is a five-shooter of the Forehand model, made by the Hopkins & Allen Company, and is of thirty-eight calibre. Detective Duke has located the store near the scene of the murder, where the negro purchased four cartridges, the exact number fired on the train when Harris was killed, thus replacing the revolver in the condition it was before the firing.

The detective has succeeded in eliciting a complete statement of the movements of the negro and his white victim on the night preceding the murder on the train, which they boarded together here. Bradley admits meeting Harris at Seventeenth, near Broad Street, and they went into a bar on or near the corner; had drinks together there; then went to another bar near the City Hall on Broad Street, and had drinks together again. Then they went into two other bars near Brooke Avenue and Broad and drank more.

KEPT ON DRINKING.

Still drinking they went to a bar near Foushee and Broad, and another drink and Harris bought a pint bottle of liquor. At the corner of Foushee and Broad Harris took charge Bradley's watch for him and $5 of his, to keep for him, as he (Bradley) was getting very drunk. Bradley's story then is that Harris had a roll of about $25 of his own in his pants pocket. The pair left Foushee and Broad together and went over to the James River division of the Chesapeake and Ohio, and walked up the track about half a mile beyond the old pump-house where they boarded the west-bound freight No. 99. They got on the same box car together and rode together until near Warminster in Nelson county. Then, according to Bradley he went to one end of the car and Harris to the other. A man came along, he said, brakeman and told him (Bradley) to get out of his way.

HE SHOT HARRIS.

This man, who, Bradley afterwards said was not a brakeman, but a man with overalls on and without a lamp, then walked up to Harris and they had some words, whereupon the man in overalls began shooting. Bradley said that as soon as the shooting commenced he went down between the cars at his end of the car, and a moment later looked up on the edge and saw blood runnng. Then he jumped off about Norwood, and went back down the track, thinking Harris had fallen off the train. He did this he said to get his watch and the $5 Harris had of his.

When Bradley was asked if he knew this man he said yes, and when asked where he first met Harris, he said it was at Iron Gate, when he (Bradley) was on his way to West Virginia to work. The second meeting was at Newport News and the third and last in Richmond the night... they boarded the train for the fatal ride. He stated that he knew Harris well, and later denied this, saying that he had never told anybody he knew the dead man's name. The negro then told a different story of the meeting with Harris the night before the tragedy. In another statement he said he was the only one on the train with Harris, and then said the man with overalls shot Harris. Bradley is a negro about twenty-four or twenty-five years of age, and is a tramp and train-beater. He claims Richmond and Nelson county as his home.

HUNG AT LOVINGSTON
Writes a Confession of His Crime—Died Repentant.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
LOUGHTON, VA. Jan. 20-Feb. 1

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
LOVINGSTON, VA., Jan. 30.—Frank Bradley, colored, paid the penalty today for the murder of W. P. Harris, of Iron Gate, on a freight train as it neared Warminster on September 10th. He left this written statement:
"When God forgives men their sins, He forgives all that they have done. I am guilty of the crime I am charged with, but I am now ready and waiting to go and rest from all my deeds. I am sorry I killed the man, and I cannot go with it in me untold.
"My mother's name is Eliza Bradley, and with my aunt, Charlotte Perkins, lives in Richmond. If I had minded them I would not be in this fix."

SHOT THE SHERIFF. A. Crawford the sheriff of
D. A. Crawford, the sheriff of Johnson county, was mortally wounded Wednesday night about dark at Claude Joiner's store by a negro named Lee Hall. The sheriff left Wrightsville early in the afternoon with a warrant for the negro, who was charged with gambling, and on reaching Joiner's store, which is about 12 miles from Wrightsville, the negro was pointed out to Mr. Crawford by Mr. Joiner. Before he could get to the negro, the latter rushed out of the store and shot the sheriff through the right lung with a 38-calibre Smith & Wesson revolver.

The latest report from the scene says that the sheriff's condition is critical. The people are very much excited and every effort is being made to capture the negro.
lee-hall-wrightsville-1903-02-07.A3:
WAS SHOT TO PIECES
NEGRO DESPERADO LYNCHED BY MOB AT WRIGHTSVILLE.
SHOT SHERIFF CRAWFORD.
JAIL DOOR BATTERED DOWN AND LEE HALL TAKEN OUT.
Mob Was Well Organized and Forced an Entrance Into Cell Occupied by Hall—Trembling Negro Dragged From Jail and Body Riddled With Bullets—Communication With Governor and Other Places Had Been Cut Off—Wounded Sheriff Will Die—Note of Warning Sent to Negro Politicians.

Wrightsville, Ga., Feb. 7.—By a well organized mob, Lee Hall, the negro who shot and mortally wounded Sheriff D. A. Crawford Wednesday, was taken from jail early this morning and lynched. Still handcuffed he was strung high in the air, and his body was riddled with bullets.

With hammers, crowbars and other instruments, work was begun on the cell door in which Hall was locked. The door was finally opened and the negro was dragged out. The mob carried him about a mile out of town to the edge of Cedar Creek, and just at the side of the public road, he was strung to a limb of a tree, and his body was riddled with bullets. The body was found there at an early hour this morning. Coroner T. L. Harris summoned a jury and held an inquest. No evidence as to the participants of the deed was produced to the jury. The verdict was that the deceased came to his death from gun and pistol shot wounds inflicted by unknown persons.

Was Well Organized.

The mob seemed to have been thoroughly organized, and prepared for every emergency. The authorities were powerless to prevent the lynching, and no communication with other places or the Governor was possible. Notices were also left warning some of the negroes most active heretofore in politics, to leave the community.

There is some apprehension of serious trouble, but the town is quiet at this time. Large crowds visited the scene of the lynching this morning, and until the body was cut down for the purpose of holding the inquest, many people from a distance remained in the neighborhood.

Hall was captured yesterday morning. Mr. Claude Joiner and other citizens who formed the posse that took Hall arrived some after dark last night and turned the prisoner over to Coroner T. L. Parris, who was acting as jailer in the interim. Feeling was running high against the negro, and after night large crowds from various places began to arrive in town. Excited groups of people could be seen on the square and public corners later during the night. About midnight the mob was organized and proceeded to the jail. A large piece of timber was secured and used as a battering ram for crushing in the outer door of the prison.

The authorities do not apprehend any outbreak beyond their control. It was thought last night that Sheriff Crawford was dead, but the latest news is to the effect that he still lives. No hopes are entertained for his recovery, however.

MOR CUT OFF HIS EARS And Fliggers, Too-Horrible Souvenirs Taken by Georgia Lynchers.
Augusta, Ga., Feb. 7.—A despatch from Wrightville, Ga., says that Lee Hall, a negro, shot and mortally wounded Sheriff D. A. Crawford last Wednesday in Washington county while Crawford was attempting to arrest him on some minor charge. Over three hundred men stormed the jail last night and took Hall out.

Half a mile from the jail in a clump of trees the men stopped and Hall was tied. His throat was cut from ear to ear, and before he had time to bleed to death over a hundred shots were fired into his body.

His ears and fingers were cut off by members of the mob as souvenirs.

Wrightsville, Ga., Feb. 7.—Lee Hall, colored, who shot and mortally wounded Sheriff D. A. Crawford, of Johnson county, last Wednesday night, was taken from the county jail here today and lynched.

ARRESTED FOR KERNS' MURDER.
Two Negroes Accuse Each Other of the Crime.
Special Dispatch to The Evening Stsr.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., January 16.—Two colored men, John E. Dryden, aged about forty years, and Lloyd Boyd, aged about fifty, were arrested yesterday by Chief of Police Brown and Officer Hubbard on the charge of fatally shooting J. J. Kerns, the United States sailor who was killed here Wednesday night. Both of the men admit being present, but each declares that the other did the shooting.

The two men were noticed together after the shooting, and they tallied with the description given by the sailors who were with Kerns. Dryden was first arrested, and immediately admitted being with the crowd when the trouble occurred, and told the police to arrest Boyd, as he did the shooting. Boyd first denied entirely being present, but afterward stated that he was there, and that Dryden fired the shot.

Kerns was taken to the Emergency Hospital after the shooting, and died there. His body was afterward removed to the Naval Academy and a coroner's inquest was held. The finding was that he came to his death from shooting by parties not yet determined.

Kerns held the rate of landsman, and before his death was stationed on board the torpedo boat destroyer Stewart, now at the academy. He had been in the navy about a year, having enlisted at Manchester, N. H. He will be buried in the naval cemetery here.
lloyd-boyd-annapolis-1903-01-16.A3:
SAILORS ON A LYNCHING BEE. Negro Murderer Hurried Out of Annapolis Killed Man on a Torpedo Boat.
BALTIMORE, Jan. 17. Although several attempts were made to lynch Lloyd Boyd, the colored murderer of J. S. Kerns of the torpedo boat Stewart, now lying at Annapolis, he was brought to this city this afternoon. Sheriff N. C. Thomas Beasley, Deputy Sheriff Nicholas W. Bryan and H. Gray Folger brought Boyd here and he is now in the city jail.

When the officers left Annapolis with their prisoner at the suggestion of State's Attorney Daniel R. Randall the excitement was intense. After the negro was locked up a large number of the sailors and marines scaled the walls of the Naval Academy and started for the jail to lynch the prisoner.

Some time afterward a large trunk was found on College avenue which had also been lifted over the academy walls, and an examination of it disclosed that it contained revolvers and dynamite. Afterward it was ascertained that an attempt would be made to blow up the jail building unless Boyd was surrendered to the mob. At forty minutes past midnight the officers took Boyd from the jail and boarded a train for this city. While on the way to Baltimore, Boyd is alleged to have made a full confession of the crime, saying that the devil got in him and made him shoot. Boyd will be kept at the city jail until the day set for his trial.

A number of colored men in the State Capital last week, organized to prevent the lynching of a colored man accused of shooting a sailor. These men deserve the greatest commendation for the manly stand they took in the matter. The jail at Annapolis is quite unsafe, and a few well directed blows from a strong man's shoulders would have opened the way to another brutal lynching. This the colored people determined to prevent, and when the authorities saw the condition of affairs, for the colored men made it plain what they intended to do, they sent the prisoner to Baltimore for safe-keeping.

We say again, all honor to the brave men of Annapolis. They deserve the praise, not only of their own people, but of the law-abiding whites of the community in which they live. All honor to the brave women who so nobly supported their husbands and their fathers in their contention for right and justice. We feel assured that not a black hand will be lifted to prevent justice from being done under the law. They are law-abiding citizens and worthy of a place in any community.
lloyd-boyd-annapolis-1903-01-16.A6:
BRAVE BLACK MEN
Determined to Protect the Prisoner at all Hazards—Wives and Sweethearts Provided Them With Refreshments-Were all Well Armed. The dispatches from Annapolis Saturday, contained an account of the burial of John J. Kearns, a white seaman, who was shot to death, so it is alleged, by a colored man, Lloyd Boyd, Janitor of the Staunton Colored School in Annapolis.

An officer of the Annapolis police force stood by and listened to a conversation between the colored man and his attorney, and then went to the Grand Jury and repeated the alleged confession of the prisoner. And strange to say the so-called confession was accepted by the Grand Jury as testimony, and the prisoner held for court under an indictment based on the officer's testimony. Such a thing is unheard of in the annals of criminal procedure.

On Saturday, Boyd was brought to Baltimore, because the authorities feared a lynching would take place. It was known at the time that a number of colored men had banded themselves together and were determined to protect the prisoner at the risk of their lives. These colored men were fully armed and were determined to sell their lives dearly. They remained in a hall in the vicinity of the jail all night, and several of their number took turns in patrolling the streets in the vicinity of the jail. The wives and female members of the families of the colored men furnished them with hot coffee and sandwiches during the night.

When it was found that the colored people of the city were determined that there should be no lynching, it was thought best to remove the prisoner to Baltimore, and put him in the jail in this city for safe keeping, and at the same time prevent trouble with the colored people. The colored men who were interested in these proceedings did not go about under cover, but plainly made known their intentions.

A number of the students at St. John's College, a state institution, climed over the walls of the college, and were preparing to join the mob of sailors and others who were contemplating taking part in the lynching. But when they heard that there was likely to be trouble, they made their way back within the walls of the school as soon as possible.

RACE WAR BREWING IN THE MILL CITY
Foolish White Girls in Company of Black Men Nearly Cause Riotus Outbreak.
Something approaching a race riot occurred at 2 o'clock yesterday morning on First avenue south and Third street, Minneapolis.

Two colored men were eating ice cream in a candy store in the company of two white girls, both, of them the daughters of respectable parents. Two white young men who are acquainted with the girls ordered the negroes to leave them. The blacks refused and there was trouble. One of the colored men was given a severe beating and the other made his escape.

A large crowd gathered on the street and there was talk of chasing the Minneapolis negroes to cover, but Patrolman Wold's arrival on the scene quelled the disturbance that was rapidly brewing. About a dozen colored men were in the vicinity, apparently ready for trouble.

After the excitement had subsided a white man standing on the sidewalk was jostled by a negro, whom he promptly knocked down. Another melee began, and for a few minutes it looked as though there would be some serious fighting. Again the interference of the police quelled the riot.

Today some of the more prominent negroes in Minneapolis have declared that if a white woman or girl wants to associate with a black man there is nothing in the law to prevent her from so doing. On the other hand, the large number of white men employed in the down-town district at night are determined to prevent the "plague from spreading," as they expressed it. There is every indication that other troubles like that of last night will occur if the belligerent black and white elements cannot be kept apart.

The negroes are making threats that if any more assaults on colored men occur they will rally to the protection of their own and use weapons in defense of their rights.

The trouble has been brought about by the fact that of late years the spectacle of negroes and white women walking and supplying together has become quite common. During the last few months, especially since the Indiana troubles and the lynchings in Southern localities, Minneapolis negroes have exhibited a special tendency to seek the society of white girls.

The police on down-town beats have been instructed to use efforts for the prevention of anything that shall savor of a race disturbance. There is no doubt that a very hostile feeling against colored men exists in the down-town district, and it is especially manifest at night.
