POLICE GET ORDERS TO STOP RACE WAR Prompt Arrests Will Follow Further Negro Beating in Minneapolis.
The police of Minneapolis are under instructions to immediately and forcibly suppress demonstrations against colored men, of which there have been several more or less aggravated instances during the last few days.

Last night Charles Collins, a St. Paul colored man employed as porter in a saloon at Washington and Hennepin, was assaulted by two unknown white men and badly bruised. There would have been a cutting affray but for the white wife of the assaulted man, who clung about his neck and was largely instrumental in preventing his use of the knife he carried.

On Thursday night a similar case of assault occurred, when two colored men were observed eating ice cream in a candy store at Third street and First avenue. Several white men assaulted the blacks, and the fight was stopped by a police officer.

The colored men who have married white women are much excited over these apparent indications of public feeling against them, and there have been several meetings of the class referred to with the object of deciding how they shall behave if attacked.

It develops that more than half of the colored waiters at the West hotel have white wives, and the same or a greater percentage exists among black waiters in nearly all the cafes and hotels of Minneapolis and St. Paul. The women who have married black men declare in the majority of cases that they are satisfied with their selections and have no complaints to make. Most of them appear anxious lest there should be further exhibitions of animosity against colored husbands of white wives, and insist that the matter of their husband's color is one that concerns the wives rather than the public.

"I have been married to my husband for eight years," said one white woman last night. "I am of Swedish parentage. I married my husband because I loved him. He has been always thoughtful of me, an excellent provider for his family, kind, good hearted to an excess, and in every way a good husband. He has never been intoxicated, he brings me every dollar he earns, we are building a little home of our own and if people mind their own business we shall always be happy together. We have children and I love them none the less because they are brown instead of white."

"The colored men in Minnesota are well behaved and hard working as a class. There are some worthless characters among them, but certainly not a greater proportion than would be found among the same number of whites. It seems to me an outrage that a few drunken rowdies who are down town at night when they ought to be in their homes, should be allowed to interfere with other men in every way respectable and hard working citizens, simply because they are black."

The dictum of Superintendent Conroy of the Minneapolis police department is that every person of whatever color who creates a disturbance on the street is to be promptly arrested and locked up. It has come to the attention of the police that a sort of feud has arisen within the last week or two between a certain class of whites and that class of colored people whose employment keeps them down town all night. The department is determined to suppress any tendency toward negro baiting in Minneapolis and persons suspected of such tendencies are being closely watched.

SLUGGED A HELPLESS MAN
Pinioned by a Policeman, a Negro Is Pounded by Excited Bystanders.
A miniature race war raged on Sixth street between Hennepin and Nicollet avenues last night and only the interference of the police prevented an affair which promised a lynching.

About 10 o'clock one of three negroes in a Sixth street saloon, after an altercation, stabbed a white man in the neck.

The three then ran out hotly pursued by a small crowd which grew rapidly and surrounded two of the negroes, the third disappearing down the street with a knife in his hand. One of the two was captured, while the other got away.

While the captured man was held by a policeman, he was repeatedly struck over the head by the excited bystanders, one of whom used a closed knife until the blood spurted from the wounded scalp.

About this time it was found that he was the wrong man and he was allowed to go, much the worse for rough handling. The white man was not seriously wounded.

WOODSTOCK HAS A SMALL TASTE OF RACE RIOT—ONLY ONE NEGRO HURT.

While a base ball game was in progress on the commons, Wednesday afternoon, between a colored ball team from Front Royal and a team from this place, Woodstock had a small taste of race war. During the most interesting part of the game a number or negro girls crowded in front of the white spectators and claimed that it was their day and that the white people would have to take a back seat. They were asked to move back, but instead of moving a young buck, Moses Banks, patroled in front of them with a base ball bat as if he was the cock of the walk. He applied a vile name to some of the small white boys, with the remark "if any white man wanted to take it up, to come out," He was accommodated, but instead of a white man taking it up a wild rush was made for him and he was beat with clubs, base ball bats and stones, which would have killed any white man. During the excitement and the rush of the crowd he made his escape and went across the commons at a 230 clip with about 75 white men and boys as close seconds. He succeeded in reaching uncle Joe Hardin's house where he hid in an up stairs room. Through respect the white people have for a respectful colored man and at the request of uncle Joe, as his wife is in a serious condition, the crowd hesitated in going into the house to bring Mr. Coon out. About that time Chief of Police Koontz and Mayor Chapman appeared on the scene and landed the young buck, in jail.

Woodstock has a large number of colored people who have the respect of every white man, woman and child in town, and this respect they are justly entitled to, but there is another class of negroes with whom we have to deal and that is the young negro bucks and the negro girls who think that their day has come. We must agree with them that their day has come to shake the dust of Woodstock from their feet and beat a hasty retreat.

The fight broke up the game in the 7th inning, with a score of 29 to 5 in favor of Front Royal.

preston-bland-new-york-1903-08-01.A1:
CROWD STONES NEGRO PRISONER.
Threatens Bland, Who Fired at Another Negro, and Hit a Passerby.
Preston Bland, a big negro longshoreman, was arraigned in the West Side court yesterday, charged with having shot William Murphy of 113 West Sixtieth street late on Saturday night. Policeman Gerhard of the West Sixty-eighth street station said he was on Amsterdam avenue near Sixty-fourth street when he heard a pistol discharged. A moment later the negro ran into the street, revolver in hand, and was knocked down and nearly killed by a trolley car. Bland dropped the revolver and a small boy made off with it.

The negro, bleeding from several cuts on the head, scrambled to his feet and ran through Sixty-fourth street to West End avenue, where Gerhard found him in a saloon. Considerable excitement was caused by the negro's flight and when Gerhard and three other cops who came to his assistance started to the station with the prisoner a crowd of a thousand had collected. They gave the policemen plenty of trouble getting Bland to Sixty-eighth street and, according to Gerhard, many stones hit the negro and the policemen.

After Bland was locked up Gerhard learned that Bland and another negro were quarrelling when Bland shot at his companion and the bullet struck a passing white man. Gerhard found Murphy in an Amsterdam avenue saloon. The bullet had passed through the fleshy part of his right arm, but he had contented himself with tying a handkerchief over the wound and was taking the highball treatment. After some protest he consented to go to the hospital and have the wound dressed. Magistrate Pool held the negro in $1,000 bail for examination to-morrow.
preston-bland-new-york-1903-08-01.A2:
HELD FOR SHOOTING WRONG MAN.
Preston Bland, a colored man, living at No. 517 Warren-st., Brooklyn, was a prisoner in the West Side Police Court yesterday, charged with shooting William Murphy, an agent, of No. 113 West Sixtieth-st., in the arm. Policeman Gerhard told the court that Bland quarrelled with another negro on Saturday night at Sixty-fourth-st. and Amsterdam-ave, and fired, missing his opponent and hitting Murphy, who was passing. Bland in running away from Gerhard, was knocked down by a trolley car and had his head cut. He was held yesterday in $1,000 bail for examination on Tuesday.

raton-raton-1903-06-11.A10:
RACE FEELING WAS HIGH. White Men Refused to Work With Colored Men at Raton Round House.
As a result of last week's heavy rains, a portion of the Santa Fe Railway's roadbed on the Blossburg spur was undermined near Blossburg, and a train toppled over on its side in passing over the place Friday. Several persons were on the train and were shaken up considerably, but no passenger was hurt. The engineer and fireman sustained painful cuts and bruises, but were not seriously hurt.

A meeting of the executive committee for the Raton Fourth of July celebration was held Thursday at Raton at which it was decided to offer liberal purses for sports, including horse races. A big display of fireworks will be given at night.

Miss Lida Burkhard, who was assistant teacher of the Raton high school last term, will be married on Wednesday, June 24, at Trinidad, Colo., to James Lawrence of the latter city.

Considerable feeling has been occasioned by the killing of Marshal Jones in Raton by the negro porter of one of the Santa Fe trains. The following day the white men of the Santa Fe round house declared that either they or the negro workmen had to get out. They then put the matter to a test and drove the colored fellows away with picks, shovels, and similar weapons.

Work on the Ratoh oil well had to be suspended last week owing to the heavy rain. The mud was so deep that coal could not be hauled to the site where the hole is being bored. An attempt was made to haul a load to the drill with a four horse wagon but the vehicle stuck in the mud and it was impossible to move it.

Carl Blazer, a Santa Fe conductor, and Miss Bessie M. Lyttle of Raton, were married in the latter town Thursday.

During a terrific electric storm at Raton last Thursday, the residences of M. R. Mendleson and A. R. Quick were struck by lightning. None of the inmates of either house was seriously injured, but all were more or less shocked.

raymond-sizer-vaughanville-1903-10-10.A1:
JUSTIFIABLE HOMICIDE.
That is the Finding of the Coroner's Jury in the Killing of Raymond Sizer by Clarence Brooks.
A. Brooks killed a negro by the name of Raymond Sizer. An inquest was held on Sunday and the jury says the killing was done in self defense. That is the story briefly told. Mr. Clarence Brooks is only seventeen years old. He had retired for the night in the store of his father where he and his brother slept. The negro aroused him to make some purchases. As the negro started out the door he made an insulting remark to Mr. Clarence Brooks and then made at him with a large iron weight and Mr. Brooks fired with the result stated, the bullet going through his heart. Only three witnesses were sworn at the inquest and their testimony is given.

The inquest was held by Magistrate J. W. Ropp at the written request of Mr. C. A. Brooks and Mr. B. W. Goodwin.

The verdict of the jury is: "That the said Raymond Sizer came to his death from a gun shot wound inflicted by the hands of Clarence M. Brooks acting in self defense—or to protect his life."

The jury was composed of J. R. Scurry, M. D. Smith, H. B. Lindsay, Jno. B. Scurry, T. R. Workman, M. J. Longshore, M. L. Connelly, S. M. Johnson, R. S. Boazman, W. J. Sullivan, Henry Workman, J. J. Amick.

A warrant was issued for Mr. Brooks and he immediately gave bond in the sum of two hundred dollars for his appearance at the sessions court to answer the charge of murder "if so deemed necessary by the solicitor."

The following is the testimony of the three witnesses sworn at the inquest:

Clarence M. Brooks, sworn, says: Live at Vaughanville, Newberry County. On 10th of October, 1903, was here sleeping in store, was in bed at 10.30 o'clock.

Negro came here knocked at the door, wanted to come in. I asked him who it was. He said "Clarence, open the door." I said, "that is not my name." He said, "what is it then." I said, "Mr. Brooks, to a negro." He came in and Walter got up and waited on him, when he got ready to go he said, "G-d d-m, Clarence Brooks wants me to call him Mr. Brooks, but I will not do it." Then I said to him he had better get out of the store.

I came on up to the door and told him to get on out. Then he said, "You G-d d-n son of a b-h, you must be a fool" and I struck him with a pistol on the side of his left face. Then he came over with a weight, I don't know when he picked it up. I told him he had better stop, he then made another step. My pistol fired. I shot him. He turned and went out and dropped the weight. He had it drawn back in his right hand this way (demonstrating.) I shot him because I thought he was going to kill me with the weight.

I am seventeen years old, weigh a hundred and thirty-five pounds. Had no difficulty before. I did not know him and had not seen him since he was small. C. M. Brooks.

Walter Brooks, sworn, says: I am fifteen years old. Clarence Brooks, my broth., was in the store when Raymond came in.

He knocked at the door and said open this door, Clarence.

Clarence said, "Don't call me Clarence." He said, "What is it then." Clarence said, "Mr. Brooks, to a negro."

I got up myself and opened the door and waited on him. When he got ready to go he said, "G-d d-n, Clarence wants me to call him Mister, but I will not do it." Clarence told him to get out of the store. He said, "I will not do it, you G-d d-n son of a b-h." He then struck Clarence and Clarence struck him with his pistol, he then picked up a weight and was coming at Clarence and Clarence told him to stop, the negro would not stop and Clarence shot him. He had it drawn back this way in his right hand. There was no one about, inside or out of the store that I know of.

Walter C. Brooks.

C. A. Brooks, sworn, says: Live at Vaughanville, Newberry County, have a store near my dwelling. The store is on my land, and was the house my sons were sleeping in at night by my directions.

Knew Raymond Sizer. He is about seventeen or eighteen years old, about the same size of Clarence, maybe better muscle, but not quite so tall. I heard the pistol fire, and came out right away. The store is about seventy-five or a hundred feet from my dwelling. I found the negro lying on the steps when I got out here, where it is now and my sons in the store. The night was clear; and nobody else was here, of if there was I could not see them. The boys are accustomed to sleeping in the store all the time when they are at home. Clar-

There was a negro meeting in progress within a short distance of the store, and it seems the leaders of the meeting gave instructions so positive that even the step-father and mother of the dead negro refused to have anything to do with the body. It must have been in obedience to such instructions for the grave had already been
raymond-sizer-vaughanville-1903-10-10.A4:
WHITE MAN KILLS A NEGRO.
Newberry, Oct. 12. — Saturday night at Vaughanville, about 18 miles from town in the upper part of this county, Clarence M. Brooks, aged about 17 years, son of Mr. C. A. Brooks, shot and instantly killed Raymond Sizer, colored, at his father's store.

The two sons of Mr. C. A. Brooks slept in the store and this negro came there and called them up and Clarence went to the door. The negro made some purchases and when he was leaving he cursed and gave Mr. Brooks some impudence, and Brooks told him to get out of the store and instead of going he picked up a weight and was about to strike Mr. Brooks when he shot him.
raymond-sizer-vaughanville-1903-10-10.A5:
RAGE TROUBLE WAS SERIOUSLY EXPECTED.
VAUGHANVILLE WAS THROWN INTO GREAT EXCITEMENT FRIDAY NIGHT.
Negro Odd Fellows Hall Was Burned--Assistance From Newberry Was Asked and Rendered.
Serious race trouble was threatened at Vaughanville, in the upper portion of the county, near the Laurens line, on Friday night. The trouble, however, seems to have passed over without other serious result than the burning of the negro Odd Fellow's hall, the members of which organization were supposed to be at the bottom of the trouble which was expected.

On Friday afternoon the report became circulated at Vaughanville that the negroes had sent to Chappells for arms, and that they would hold a meeting at the Odd Fellows' hall Friday night, after which they would wait on young Clareuce M. Brooks, who on Saturday night a week ago shot and killed a negro, Raymond Sizer, as the coroner's jury said, in self-defense, and that they would also call upon the gentlemen who helped to bury Sizer. The account of this shooting, together with the evidence taken at the coroner's inquest, was published in The Herald and News at the time. Sizer was a prominent member of the negro lodge of Odd Fellows, which has long been a disturbing element in the community. It will be remembered that after the inquest Sizer's relatives or any other negroes refused to touch the body, and that a coffin was made and the body buried by the white people, the members of the coroner's jury and young Brooks' attorney, Mr. Cole. L. Blease, assisting in the interment. The relatives of the dead negro had ordered a coffin from Cross Hill, but turned it back when it reached Vaughanville. Next day after the body was buried by the white people the negroes opened the grave, placed the body in another coffin, and reburied it at a point about a mile distant from the first grave. The reason for this action and why the negroes should wish to call upon the white men who buried the body, is unexplained.

Since Sizer's death the negro Odd Fellows, of which he was a member, have held very frequent meetings, a representative of The Herald and News was informed by the people of Vaughanville, and have made numerous threats. These threats, taken in connection with the reports which became circulated Friday afternoon, caused great excitement in the community, and serious trouble was feared.

A 'phone message was sent to Newberry for assistance at about four o'clock Friday afternoon, and a party of twelve immediately left for Vaughanville, twenty-one miles distant. When the Newberry party, accompanied by a representative of The Herald and News, arrived on the scene, there was no indication of trouble, except there were about thirty five white men in the little store of Mr. Whit Goodwyn, armed to the teeth with double-barrelled shot guns and small arms, and prepared to meet any trouble which might occur. The addition of the Newberry party made about fifty.
raymond-sizer-vaughanville-1903-10-10.A6:
A meeting was called to order by Mr. Cole L. Blease and the situation was discussed. A detachment of twelve men was sent to the Odd Fellows' hall at about 9 o'clock to see if the expected meeting of negroes would be held. There was no light in the building and no one was found.

Shortly after the prrty returned to the store, the building, a loosely constructed, two-story frame structure, was seen to be ablaze, and it soon burned to the ground. The conflagration lighted up the country for miles around. The building was the property of the negro Odd Fellows and was not of any great value. The first floor was used for a negro school. It was situated about a quarter of a mile from Mr. Goodwyn's store and was near an old negro church. The fire occurred some time before 11 o'clock. How it started is not known.

The situation was again discussed. It was proposed to visit the negroes who are supposed to be the ringleaders and to give them correction, but this motion was immediately opposed by Mr. Fred H. Dominick, who was seconded by Mr. Blease and the officers of the law, Deputy Sheriff Duncan Johnson and Constable C. G. Blease, and the proposal was almost unanimously voted down, the gentlemen present saying emphatically they had come to protect the white people of the community and young Brooks, and not to create a disturbance.

It was feared that trouble might result later in the night, and it was decided that the men should sleep under arms, and sentinels were posted. A number slept in the store and the others in the surrounding homes.

The representative of The Herald and News called upon young Brooks' father. Mr. Brooks said he was convinced that, had not prompt action been taken and assistance received, the negroes would have attempted hurt to his family, and especially his son, during the night.

Nothing unusual developed during the night and next morning most of the party returned to their homes, several remaining in case any further trouble occurred.

The negro Odd Fellows, whose hall was burned, The Herald and News man was informed by the people of Vaughanville, has exercised a baneful influence over the negroes of the community since their organization several years ago. The names of Isaac Fortune, Jones Pitts, West Bates, Jim Wade and Ben Watts were given as the ringleaders. It is said the hall has been used as a general assembly hall for the negroes, where they met under the mantle of secrecy and hatched their schemes without fear of interruption. When a representative of The Herald and News passed by the site of the hall on his return home Saturday morning, the embers were still smouldering. Posted around on the trees were notices, signed by officers of the lodge, warning all against smoking on the premises. This is the third race trouble threatened at Vaughanville in recent years. Several years ago it
raymond-sizer-vaughanville-1903-10-10.A7:
uprising and there was a great deal of excitement for a time, with the result that the doctor was run out of the community. A year later the same experience was repeated with another negro doctor, J. W. T. Patterson, with the same result.

Clarence Brooks, the young man who killed the negro Sizer, and whose act was the cause of the threatened negro uprising, is the seventeen-year-old son of Mr. C. A. Brooks. He is under $200 bond and it is said will be prosecuted.

It is a matter of congratulation to the people of the community and the whole county, that the affair on Friday night ended with so little serious results. Had there been any demonstration by the negroes there is no doubt that blood would have been freely spilt. All is quiet for the present, but it is not know at what time the trouble will break out again.

NEGRO REPORTED KILLED.

It has been reported on the streets of Newberry and elsewhere throughout the county that early Friday night a negro, carrying a lighted lantern, was seen near the Odd Fellows' hall, and that when he was questioned and replied that he was a black man, he was fired upon and killed. A representative of The Herald and News reached the scene shortly after 8 o'clock Friday night and remained until 7 o'clock Saturday morning, and no such act came within his notice. It may be that some one was fired upon, but it appears that the report that any one was killed is unfounded.

AN ORDERLY CROWD.

The party that went up to Vaughanville from Newberry went to protect the people of Vaughanville if it should be necessary and not to create a disturbance, and the Newberry party kept strictly within the purpose for which it went.
raymond-sizer-vaughanville-1903-10-10.A10:
CLARENCE BROOKS QUICKLY ACQUITTED
WAS CHARGED WITH MURDER OF NE GRO SIZER.
The Jeter Case Entered Upon Late Yesterday Afternoon- Other Cases In Court.
The court of general session has had most of its time consumed with only a few cases, full reports of which appear elsewhere.

The case against young Clarence M. Brooks, charged with the murder of the negro Raymond Sizer, was taken up yesterday afternoon. There was very little testimony. Brooks was promptly acquitted. This is the Vaugianville case.

The case against R. R. Jeter was next taken up late yesterday afternoon.

McD. Heller and Dora Heller were convicted of fornication.

Robert Johnson, colored was convicted of carrying unlawful weapons and sentenced to pay a fine of $15 or to serve thirty days.

robert-good-mcgehee-1903-07-03.A1:
BAD ROBERT GOOD.
Objected to Ejectment From Train and Killed a Passenger.
Objected to Ejectment From Train and Killed a Passenger.

Little Rock, Ark., July 3.—A special to The Gazette from McGehee, Ark., says: B. L. Wright was accidentally shot and killed on a passenger train here today by a boisterous negro passenger whom the porter was endeavoring to put off the train.

Robert Good, the negro, had threatened the porter and the latter drew a revolver which Good succeeded in taking from him and firing. The bullet struck and instantally killed Wright who was in an adjoining car.

Good escaped, but was overtaken by a posse and killed while resisting arrest. Wright was a thirty-second degree Mason. His home was at Alexander, La. He was a passenger conductor in the service of the Iron Mountain road.
robert-good-mcgehee-1903-07-03.A2:
CONDUCTOR SHOT DOWN BY A NEGRO MAN.
Citizens of McGhee, Ark., Aroused by the Killing of "Bun" Wright Near There on Train.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.
Pine Bluff, Ark., July 3.—All Southeast Arkansas is aroused to-night over the killing of Conductor "Bun" Wright, which occurred at McGhee this afternoon at 3 o'clock.

Wright had charge of passenger train No. 66 on the Southern Division of the Valley Route of the Iron Mountain. He interrupted a wrangle between two negroes over a pistol, and John Goodwin, a brown-skin negro, shot and killed Wright. The negro then immediately fled to the woods.

Jefferson County authorities here were notified, and at 6 o'clock Sheriff Gould, two deputies and bloodnounds departed on a special train for the scene of the crime. If the negro is captured he may be lynched, as railway operatives and McGhee citizens are wrought up to a high pitch.

Wright was highly regarded by all who knew him. He had been on the division about four months. His father is an engineer on the Fort Smith division, out of Fort Smith. The dead man lived at Little Rock.
robert-good-mcgehee-1903-07-03.A7:
TRAGEDY ON A TRAIN
Unfortunate Termination of a Difficulty in Arkansas.
INNOCENT MAN DEAD
Porter and a Negro Passenger Were Struggling For Possession of a Pistol, That Went Off and Killed a Mr. Wright.
Little Rock, Ark., July 4.—A special to the Arkansas Gazette from McGehee, Ark., says:

B. L. Wright of Alexandria, La., was accidentally shot and instantly killed at 3 o'clock Friday afternoon by Robert Good, a negro. Good was scuffling with the train porter, George Davis, who pulled a gun. Good took the gun away from him and fired at close range. The men were in the end of the car and the bullet crashed through the glass door of the car and entered the wooden door of the baggage car, striking Wright, who was tsanding in the middle of the car, in the neck, breaking it. He fell back in his wife's arms and expired. The porter and Good came out of the car and fell to the platform as the train entered the station. At the point of a gun a passenger made Good give up the gun and he ran down the railroad, followed by several shots. Then it was found that Wright had been killed.

The train was held here while an inquest was held, the verdict being that Wright was murdered by Robert Good.

A score of posses set out to search for Good, and late in the afternoon he was cornered and shot to death while resisting arrest.

Wright's body was placed in the baggage car on a stretcher and taken to Little Rock, where it was prepared for burial. The interment will be at Fort Smith where his father resides.
robert-good-mcgehee-1903-07-03.A8:
The Fourth of July celebration started in Pine Bluff and vicinity early, in fact, a day ahead, and by 6:05 a.m., had three killings and one man dangerously shot.

Tragedy No. 1.

The first of the four tragedies to occur, was the killing of Bud Wright, an Iron Mountain conductor, at McGhee, south of Pine Bluff, by John Goodwin, a negro. Wright was conductor on a local freight train. The killing occurred at 3:30 p. m.

The wife and children of Conductor Wright were on the train en route to Little Rock, to spend the Fourth. Near McGhee, John Goodwin, a negro, boarded the train. He was noisy and inclined to be quarrelsome. The porter told him he must keep quiet or be put off the train. Instead of Goodwin becoming quiet, he became enraged at what the porter said, and the two became engaged in a scuffle in which the porter drew a pistol, which Goodwin snatched from the porter's hand and fired on the porter with it. He missed his mark, but the bullet passed through two doors and struck Conductor Wright in the neck, producing almost instant death. Wright was seated with his family in the car, and they were eating a lunch.
robert-good-mcgehee-1903-07-03.A9:
Tragedy No. 2.
After taking the fatal shot, Goodwin leaped from the train and took to the woods. The news soon spread over the little town of McGhee, and the citizens began to plan how to capture Goodwin. Two men suspected that Goodwin would take a circuitous route to reach his home, and they armed themselves with double-barrel shot-guns, went near Goodwin's home, and waited for him to put in an appearance. After dark Goodwin showed up, and four charges of buckshot were turned loose on him and all four must have been effective as Goodwin fell with his head nearly all torn off.

Wright's train came on to Pine Bluff and the county and railroad officials notified of the killing. The Pine Bluff-Little Rock train was made up as a special, with engine, baggage car and one coach. Conductor P. D. Atwood was in charge of the special, and engineer Molter and fireman Hondlette were in the cab. The train made the run from here to McGhee, sixty miles, in an hour and thirty-five minutes. On the train were Sheriff Gould and deputies Philpot, Dunlap and Tom Meeks, with the county bloodhounds. But when the train reached McGhee, it was too late for hunting Goodwin with any intention of arresting him, as he had been killed in the manner stated in the foregoing.

The special train returned to Pine Bluff, and the officers reported the killing as herewith told, but said they were unable to learn who the two men were that killed Goodwin. The Graphlc received a special telegram Saturday from Monticello which says:

"Negro who killed Conductor Wright yesterday, resisted arrest and was killed by Hugh Henry."

The remains of Wright were sent to Fort Smith for interment. Wright was a popular railroad man, and had been on this division of the Iron Mountain for about four months. He was born and reared at Fort Smith and his home was still at Fort Smith.
robert-good-mcgehee-1903-07-03.A10:
Conductor Wright Killed by a Stray Bullet Fired by a Drunken Negro.
EVENTS OF A WEEK BRIEFLY CHRONICLED
Quarterly Report of State Land Commissioner—Section of Game Law Forbidding Non-Residents Hunting on Their Own Lands Declared Unconstitutional.
Conductor's Sad Death. I. Wright, a conductor or
B. L. Wright, a conductor on the lower end of the Valley Route, was accidentally shot and killed by John Goodwin, a negro, as a passenger train upon which himself and family were en route to Little Rock entered the station of McGehee. Wright was standing near the door of the baggage car. Goodwin, who was in the colored coach, had become boisterous and drew a pistol. The train porter grappled with him and in the scuffle Goodwin's revolver was discharged. The bullet went through the glass door of the colored coach and on through the wooden door of the baggage car, striking Wright in the neck. His wife and two children were also with him in the baggage car, and the unfortunate man expired in his terrified wife's arms without uttering a word, the bullet breaking his neck. The train porter succeeded in shoving Goodwin from the car platform, and when it became known that Wright had been killed a posse started after the murderer. He was located in a house about four miles from McGehee and upon his refusal to surrender, was shot to death. Wright's remains were prepared for burial at Little Rock and forwarded to Fort Smith for interment.

The Savannah Tribune.
SATURDAY MARCH 28,1903 ALL believers of just ce and fair play have been commending President Roosevelt for his attitude toward the race. As predicted, our poor people are being fleeced by smooth tongue rascals on the plea of the passage of the ex-slave pension bill. THE separate car law in this state would no doubt be more satisfactory if white men were not allowed in the coach allotted to colored passengers. THE legislature of Missouri has refused to enact a separate car law. The legislature of this state contains many members who are not tainted with race prejudice. EACH morning there is a curious crowd of men and women who attend the recorder's court. What is true of this court is also true of the other courts when in session. This idle and curious class should find more profitable employment. THERE are some members of the police force who are adepts at using the club on the head of colored men whom they have under arrest. Under the regime of that fearless and just recorder, Mr. H. E. Wilson, this ornal practice was abolished, but at present the police are upheld in whatever they do in this respect. In certain sections of the city small white boys generally gather and at times interfere with colored persons in passing. This interference on the part of this lawless element may yet terminate into serious trouble. This nearly happened on Sunday afternoon when several ladies were mistreated. The boys who were guilty were docketed. They were also punished by their parents. Whenever these boys act in any manner unbecoming they should be reported, because if they are allowed to continue the practice they will become bolder and commit offenses that may be more serious. In the south ninety per cent of the supporters of the Republican party are among the colored people. In the northern and western parts this per cent, and especially in some states, is very small. In the distribution of patronage it is always necessary to give preference to those who are the main supporters of the party. For that reason there are more colored men appointed to positions of honor and emolument in this section than elsewhere. It must not be misunderstood that there are not many colored men holding lucrative positions who have been appointed from sections other than the south. Some of the southern daily papers have
reason there are more colored men appointed to positions of honor and emolument in this section than elsewhere. It must not be misunderstood that there are not many colored men holding lucrative positions who have been appointed from sections other than the south. Some of the southern daily papers have been asking why the President does not appoint colored men as collectors of customs in northern and western ports. In asking this they are merely begging the question. Those journals should understand that if conditions were the same in these sections as in the south such appointments would be made. These journals are not in favor of colored man holding office anywhere. It is fully decided by them and many southernners that the only "door of hope" that they would be willing to have open to the colored man, is the farm. They will find many colored men to stick to the farm and get along prosperously to, but in the other avenues of life they will never be able to debar him. The only thing that the white man will be able to succeed in preventing the colored man from becoming, is a social companion, and in that direction the colored man is not aspiring, and toward it show feeling akin to the white man. This country is the black man's as well as the white man's. It has been developed by both races. The black man has fledled the forrests, opened highways, reclaimed swamps, tilled the soil, and assisted in making this the greatest country on earth. He is going to continue in this development. He is going to stay right here, better his condition and as heretefore live a model citizen with the one request to be let alone with unabridged rights of citizenship.

st-paul-st-paul-1903-08-23.A1:
SHE FIRES THRICE AND NEGRO FLEES

Miss Mary Hagan Adopts Heroic Measures With Man Who Affronts Her.
Miss Mary M. Hagan who, with her brother Percy, conducts the St. Paul Messenger and Express company, was attacked by an unknown colored man last night at 11:30 o'clock at the corner of Eighth and Sibley streets, and she promptly put him to flight by firing three shots at him.

Miss Hagan says that she has been troubled by the negro following her when she goes to her home each night from the messenger office, where she is busy till after 11 o'clock. She said that he had frequently frightened her as she was walking alone and she determined to resort to means to protect herself.

"I took a revolver with me more to scare him off than anything else," said Miss Hagan. "But when he grabbed me by the arm I got so frightened that I discharged the revolver three times. I do not think that I struck him, though as he ran away I saw him take a handkerchief from his pocket and place it up against the side of his face. He ran away so quickly that I did not see any indication of a wound."

A crowd quickly gathered on hearing the reports of the revolver, and great excitement prevailed. Several men, on learning the direction taken by the fleeing negro, ran after him, and would have used summary methods had they overtaken him.

Several of the gentlemen in the crowd offered to escort Miss Hagan to her home, but she tharked them and said that she did not fear that the negro would appear again.

VINELAND HAS RACE CLASH.
Vineland, N. J., July 27.—A general fight between whites and blacks which nearly resulted in a riot, was occasioned here last night by the interference of John Shockley, a colored officer, and a colored man by the name of Thomas, trying to separate Albey Welser and Harry Loper while wrestling on a street corner.

The officer arose and, pulling his revolver, pointed it at Tony Robinson and fired. But for his bad aim the shot would have proven fatal. Robinson knocked Shockley down and the other negro started through the crowd of about 500 and knocked people right and left.
Harry Loper, picking up a chair, hit Thomas as he passed and broke the rounds over his head. Thomas, amid the cries of the mob for his life, rushed up the street and disappeared through the yard of the Unitarian Church, two blocks away, barely escaping with his life. Robinson was placed under arrest for assaulting the officer, and this morning plead not guilty to the charge.

Shockley was placed under arrest last night for shooting at Robinson, and Thomas was locked up upon his appearance in this city this morning.

Welser and Loper, over whom the trouble arose, say they were simply having a little fun and not fighting, as is claimed by Shockley.

Fred Tutcher, the young man who was brutally shot down by a negro Sunday night, died at 4:15 Monday afternoon at Christ hospital from the effects of the wound. At 2:45 o'clock in the afternoon he was seized with convulsions, but rallied an hour later and called for his mother. She had barely reached his bedside at Christ hospital when he died with a hemorrhage. The dying scene was a very sad one, and the hospital attendants, who are accustomed to seeing grief and suffering, were moved to tears. After calling upon her son to look at her, the heartbroken mother raised his eyelids so that he might see her for the last time. He was conscious, but unable to speak or open his eyes.

In the crowd which assembled around the city jail after dark, there were a large number who did not know that the body of the murdered boy was at Shellabarger's undertaking establishment just across the street. The assembly could not be called a mob. It consisted of spectators, to the number of three or four hundred, who were there to see if any demonstration would be made. But it was an assembly of spectators who would have joined any organized mob, no matter how small. The fact that there were no leaders saved trouble.

The two negroes who committed the dastardly crime were not in town, having been spirited away to Lawrence before dark by Sheriff Lucas, but a number of officers were kept around the station for the purpose of quelling any street riot which might occur between white and negroes. This was the only danger. The whites were quiet and peaceable, and not a weapon of any kind was displayed among them, although it is probable that a number of them had revolvers, and would have used them if trouble had been started. On the other hand, crowds of negroes assembled carrying shotguns, rifles and revolvers conspicuously displayed. They showed an aggressive spirit and a desire to pick a quarrel with the whites. They mixed in the general crowd, and a white man passing though had to be careful to avoid being tripped up by some negro. For a few minutes, about 10 o'clock, when the crowd of whites began to fully realize that the negroes were hunting trouble, things were in such a condition that a loud voice or a slight altercation would have precipitated a fight. The negroes then backed off into dark corners, and the whites began to disperse. At 11:30 all the whites were gone, but a number of armed negroes were still in sight. Several policemen who had been called in from their beats went away to their regular work, and Chief Goff went home. When the crowd was the thickest some of the policemen who had noticed that many negroes were carrying shotguns and rifles, advocated arresting and disarming them, but Chief Goff forbade them to do so. "Although they are making the demonstration and exhibiting their weapons," he said, "they would declare that we were showing favoritism, and that the whites were also armed, and I think if you would search a lot of those white men you would find that they were right. Let them alone. If anything is started, let them start it. It is our business to stop a disturbance, not to create one," which is rather an amusing view of the duties of the police as applied to an impending conflict.

In their confession the two negroes, Will Mason and Thomas DeMoss, said that they were acting in self-defense, as the murdered man was coming at them with a club. There is nothing to corroborate their statement. P. L. Reed, who saw the tragedy, says that Tutcher had nothing in his hands, and made no attempt to strike either of his assailants.

The ante-mortem statement of Tutcher, which was taken at the hospital by County Attorney Hungate while the boy was dying, follows the story in detail as told by Reed. It is as follows:

I am now lying at Christ hospital, Topeka, Shawnee county, Kansas, and I make the following statement as my ante-mortem statement of how I received the injury from which I am now suffering. New York, Oct. 20.—William C. Crehan, formerly a well known theatrical manager, is dead at his home in this city. He retired four years ago and since then devoted his time to music and painting. Crehan was a brother of Miss Ada Rehan. He was born in Ireland 59 years ago.

Mother Gets Her Children Back.

San Francisco, Oct. 20.—Mrs. J. S. Buck has just returned to this city from New York with her two children who had been abducted by their father several months ago The boy is nine and the girl seven years old. Buck suddenly disappeared one day with his children, leaving the mother penniless. Mrs. Buck pluckily went to work, accumulated $200, and with the assistance of the California society for the prevention of cruelty to children, located her husband and, children on a farm at Mina, N. FIRST DEGREE MURDER
Coroner's Jury in Tutcher Case Makes Its Report.
Will Mason and Thomas DeMoss, the two negroes who murdered Fred Tutcher, are charged with murder in the first degree, and will be brought back from Lawrence for a preliminary hearing after the funeral of their victim. County Attorney Hungate says there is plenty of evidence to substantiate a charge of first degree murder, and that the crime was undoubtedly premeditated. "Premeditation" does not necessitate a day or week of careful planning before a crime is committed. It has been clearly shown that the negro, Mason, after drawing his revolver and telling Tutcher that he would kill him, waited for his companion to get out of the way before firing the shot. Both men will be tried as equally guilty. The coroner's jury at the inquest yesterday brought in a verdict to the effect that Fred Tutcher came to his death as the direct result of a gunshot wound, the bullet being fired from a revolver held in the hand of Will Mason.

The funeral of Fred Tutcher will be held from the home of his parents, 1249 Polk street, at 3 o'clock Thursday afternoon. By that time his sister Maud, who lives in Spokane, Wash., is expected to arrive. Another sister, Mollie Tutcher, has arrived from Denison, Tex. Three other sisters, Jessie, Nellie and Hazel, are at home.

There were but two sons in the family, and they both died of gunshot wounds. The eldest son, Will Tutcher, was among the Americans killed by boxers in China during the war. He was a soldier in the army which stormed Pekin.

The man who murdered his wife at the Reform school was also apprehended at once by the officers and is now waiting trial. Several murders have been committed here in the last few years, all of whom have been captured by the officers and speedily dealt with according to law. william-mason-topeka-1903-10-19.A17:
THE TUTCHER MURDER.
The murder of Fred Tutcher, a young man who had a reputation for attending to his own business by two drunken negroes this week was inhuman and wholly without justification. The shooting was unprovoked and there wasn't the least semblance of extenuation.

There was a sentiment among the people of Topeka favoring the lynching of the two miserable wretches who perpetrated the dastardly murder but fortunately it subsided without a show of mob law. A community gains nothing by taking the law into its own hands. It may result in terrorizing the lawless element for a time but in the end the moral effect on the community at large is demoralizing. There are few people who will say that these men do not deserve hanging but meeting one murder with another would not bring the victim back to life nor lighten the burden of grief which the family of the young man must sustain.

Topeka may congratulate itself that the danger of a disgraceful lynching has been averted and that the law is to be allowed to take its course.

There is another feature in the Tutcher murder that may well be considered. It is the evidence of wantonness among young men, white and black that crops out so often in every community. It is altogether likely that Mason and DeMoss, when they started out "for a time" last Sunday, had no thought of murder in their minds. Still they were armed and when an occasion presented itself they did not hesitate to shoot down an innocent man. It was apparently done in a spirit of wantonness which comes from an unnatural and perverted idea of the purpose of human life. There are too many young men in Topeka who are like Mason and DeMoss in a greater or less degree.

The head-hunting Dyak of Borneo, who, by processes peculiar to the black races, reduces the head of his slain enemy to the size of a small orange, without spoiling its contours or recognizability, will sometimes sell to a white man a specimen of his grisly skill. Trial of Wm. Mason, for the Crime, Begins.
Separate Trials Demanded for the Two Defendants.
THE DYING STATEMENT
Question About Its Admission as Evidence.
Little Trouble Experienced in Securing a Jury.
The trial of William Mason, colored, charged with shooting Fred Tutcher the night of October 18, was called for trial in the district court this morning.

William Mason and Thomas DeMoss were arrested charged with the killing of Tutcher. The two defendants demanded separate trials and County Attorney Hungate elected to try Mason first.

Mason was represented by Attorney J. S. Ensminger. Mason's father and brother sat with him in the court room. County Attorney Hungate and Assistant County Attorney McNary conducted the prosecution. Fred Tutcher's father sat behind the county attorney.

The case was called at 10 o'clock and the 40 special veniremen to be called to the witness box in case they were needed were in the court room. The regular jurymen were the first examined. The state asked the usual questions but Attorney Ensminger was careful and thorough in his examination of the jurymen. He attempted to draw out the fact that the jurymen had formed an opinion but up to noon but one juryman was called who announced that he had formed an opinion.

The jurymen examined had all heard of the shooting, except two who had not heard of it until they were called to serve on the jury.

M. Snattinger thought he had an impression as to the shooting but he had not formed a fixed opinion. Attorney Ensminger objected to him as a juror, but the court overruled the objection.

The taking of testimony in the case will likely begin this afternoon, and the evidence for the prosecution can all be submitted by Tuesday afternoon. The defense will probably be on the ground of self-defense. The evidence for the defense will not require more than a day. The trial is expected to be finished before Thursday, when the Lowe murder case is to be called for hearing.

County Attorney Hungate has in his possession the confession made by Mason soon after he was arrested and while he was in jail. He feared that a mob might try to get him. If the prosecution attempts to introduce the confession the defense will oppose it on the ground that the confession was made while the defendant was in fear of violence at the hands of a mob.

The prosecution will also introduce the antemortem statement made by Fred Tutcher. Tutcher signified his wish to make a statement. He was too weak to talk. P. L. Reed, who was a witness to the shooting, recited the events as he saw them. Tutcher nodded his assent to the statements and signed the record of the shooting as recited by Reed.

Reed will be the principal witness for the prosecution. His testimony will be substantiated by the confession made by Mason and the statements made by DeMoss to the officers and the antemortem statement of Tutcher.

Tutcher was engaged in the livery business, with his father, at the southeast corner and Seventh and VanBuren streets. On Sunday afternoon, October 18, Mason and DeMoss hired a buggy from the stable. They did not return until nearly midnight. They drove into the stable at a fast pace. The horse bore evidence of hard driving. Fred Tutcher was on duty at the barn that night. P. L. Reed was the only person with him. Tutcher rebuked Mason and DeMoss for abusing the horse by hard driving. Mason jumped out of the buggy, drew a revolver, told DeMoss to stand aside and he shot Tutcher in the abdomen. At the time DeMoss was threatening to strike Tutcher with a whip. Mason and DeMoss fled and were captured the next day by the police. For fear of mob violence they were taken to Lawrence. A mob gathered at the city jail on the night of October 19 but dispersed when it was found that the prisoners had been taken away.

Tutcher died at Christ's hospital the day after the shooting.

William Mason is a black skinned negro. He stands about five feet ten inches and weighs about 190 pounds. His mouth is comparatively small. His lips are unusually thick and protruding. He was dressed in a blue sweater and a dark suit of clothes. He paid little attention to the securing of the jury.

PENALTY OF DEATH.
It Will Be Pronounced but Never Executed.
Prisoner Is Handcuffed and Returned to Prison.
The jury, which heard the evidence in the case of William Mason, colored, charged with the murder of Fred Tutcher on the night of Sunday, October 18, left the jury box in the district court this morning at 11:02 o'clock and at 11:21 o'clock returned a verdict finding Mason guilty of murder in the first degree. The penalty, prescribed by law, is death by hanging. As is the custom Mason will be sentenced to the state penitentiary, there to remain until such time as the governor of the state may fix for the carrying out of the execution.

Captain H. X. Devendorf was chosen foreman of the jury. After the verdict had been read Attorney Ensminger for Mason demanded that the jury be polled. Each man was asked separately if the verdict was his and if he was satisfied. Each juryman responded that the verdict was correct.

When the verdict had been delivered and Judge Hazen dismissed the jury, there was no demonstration of any sort in the court room. A large crowd was in attendance, mostly negroes. Sheriff Lucas and Jailor Lawson approached Mason to take him back to the county jail. Lawson drew a pair of handcuffs from his pocket. Mason held out his hands, laughed aloud and allowed the handcuffs to be placed on his wrists.

Mason evidenced no concern during the trial. He sat with a stolid expression, his lips protruding and his eyes half closed. Mason's father and brother were with him and they seemed no more concerned than the defendant.

Captain J. R. McNary opened the argument for the prosecution this morning. He was followed by Attorney Ensminger. County Attorney Hungate made the closing argument in the case.

In the Mason murder case the record for speedy justice was made in Shawnee county. The crime was committed on the night of October 18. Fred Tutcher died at Christ hospital on October 19. Mason and DeMoss were captured on October 19. The defendants waived their preliminary hearing in the city court. The case went to the district court and 50 days after the murder was committed Mason was before a jury on trial for his life.

The case was called in the district court Monday morning at 10 o'clock and Tuesday morning shortly after 11 o'clock the case was ended and the jury had returned a verdict of guilty.

The defense attempted to prove self-defense and to raise a doubt in hopes that a verdict of murder in the second degree might possibly be secured. The jurymen who heard the case were as follows: J.
